translations.text: Again: Other topics concerning the soul and the distinction between human passions—bodily, of the soul, and spiritual.
Now I, Eutropius, and Eusebius, after receiving his first letter, made arrangements to come to him.
When we entered his cell and greeted one another with prayer, many things were said in our conversation with one another that were not written down.
Our first question was this: Why, out of all bodies, was the nature of the soul placed in the human body? The Solitary said:
My dear friends, I will speak according to how the matter appears to me. Because God wished to train the human being alone in the knowledge of his wisdom,
he established for him this whole natural world, broad and spacious in its height and depth, although its elements are opposed to one another by nature.
Within its deep hollow and the circuit of its sphere, he established dimensions for its regions through the division of the seas,
the running of rivers, the flowing of springs, the growth of trees, and forms of every color;
and within the vault of the firmament, the shining of the heavenly lights in high and low places, at the differing times of the sun and moon.
And because everything that moves in its course and has color in its appearance exists in two mysteries—in its visible appearance and in the skill of God's workmanship within it—
therefore, the being whom God was about to create, whom these created things would serve and whom they would bring to an understanding of his wisdom,
had to have his existence in the world through two activities belonging to two substances,
so that this visible substance of the body might delight in the visible appearance of these wonderful beauties that shine out from all created things,
and this hidden substance of the soul might delight in the wisdom concealed within them.
For if he gave created things an imprint and a form in the color of their outward appearance, and a hidden mystery concealed within them that reveals God's wisdom,
how much more would he establish the human being, the king of all the things in this creation, in the surpassing beauty of the form of his bodily members,
and in a glorious nature active within him for understanding God's works! Eusebius said:
Could not the body itself, through the activity of its senses, have been sufficient to understand the arrangement of these works? The Solitary said:
The nature of the body cannot see with the sight of the eyes something that can be seen only with the mind.
For look: the eyes themselves cannot see above the firmament. And when we wish to look above the firmament,
we do not look with bodily eyes, but contemplate with the mind within. And it is not the gaze of the pupils that enters inside a house, but that of the heart.
And when the full moon rises from the east, it appears to the eyes to be less than five miles away. But the mind understands that it is to the east of everyone.
And because the outward senses could not, through hearing, sight, smell, and touch, explore the inward mystery of created things,
God therefore conceals within the hidden recesses of the inward members a nature whose perceptions are subtler than those of all bodies,
so that, through the keenness and subtlety of its activities, it might explore the concealed wisdom of the things brought into being by the Lord of all. Eusebius said:
And would souls not have been able, while existing separately without a body, to understand the wisdom of God? Just as
the angels, although they have no bodies, are powerful in their understanding of God and have no need for a body to serve as a means for them,
so too those souls could have contemplated the wisdom of God without being placed in a body.
The Solitary says: My brothers, if those souls had been created in such a manner that they would exist in the world without bodies,

their knowledge would have been sufficient for them to perceive the hidden wisdom of these created natures. Yet they would not have been moved to investigate them, because their own nature is higher than theirs.
They have no need of them. And because they have no need of them, they would not concern themselves with the wisdom within them either,
just as the seraphim do not concern themselves with investigating the wisdom of this world, because their nature is higher than it.
And since you brought forward the nature of the angels as an example, a different mystery applies to them: they remain in the order in which God created them.
But the nature of souls was not established in this way by God. And if a human being were only a body without a soul,
God would have made in the world not a human being as such, but a body like the other bodies that lack understanding of his wisdom, like the kinds of animals and the birds of the sky.
The whole distinction of a human being from all other created natures lies in the honor bestowed on him through the soul within him.
And because the soul is within him, his afflictions and his dependence on everything stir it within him to gain wisdom about everything.
The body shares with the soul in the discoveries that come from it, and the soul shares with the body in the wisdom hidden within it, in its coming into being from God.
And if a human being were without a soul, he would be like everything else, as I said above.
And if souls had been created in the world without bodies, it would have been pointless for them, needing none of the created natures, to be stirred to thoughts about their constitution.
But now that they have been clothed in bodies, the body has become their reason for thinking about bodily things.
And because of it, they concern themselves with the wisdom within it, in every person and in varying degrees. Eusebius says:
I would like to hear how souls are above dependence on everything visible. The Solitary says:
Look and consider the service of all the things through which every need of the body is met, while the soul has no need of them.
For it is not something visible, so as to depend on visible things: not on the rising of the sun, nor on the changes of the moon,
nor on all the movement in the region above us—that is, not on the density of the clouds, nor on the fire of lightning,
nor on the sound of thunder, nor on downpours of rain, nor on the flow of springs, nor on the light of day, nor on the stillness of night,
nor on the seasons of the mountains, nor on the counting of hours, nor on the changing of months, nor on the cycle of the whole year and everything that takes place in it.
Rather, the soul's nature is free from all these things, so that through its subtle movements human beings may investigate the wonder of God's works.
But instead of concerning themselves with this pursuit, so that through constant attention to it they might be restrained from bodily desires, they have wronged God through improper deeds.
They reflect neither on the wisdom of nature nor on the wisdom of the Scriptures. Oh, how much care God has taken to make human beings wise!
Oh, how far they have withdrawn from the discipline of his teaching! They concern themselves only with worthless things.
For anyone who takes pleasure only in seeing natural things with his outward sight, but does not care to investigate the wisdom of God within them, stands on the same level as the animals.
They too, like him, see with their outward senses the sun, the moon, the stars, the light, and all the colors on earth. But anyone who concerns himself with
the hidden wisdom within them is a person of the soul, who gazes with the senses of his soul upon the handiwork of the Lord of all. Eusebius says:
“What has been said on this subject, concerning the reason for the soul’s dwelling in the body, is enough for us. But because we wish to hear many things,
which will also benefit our souls, we ask you to explain to us the conduct of the inner and the outer person.” The Solitary says:
“I will begin by speaking first about the divine commandment that brings us near to love for him: ‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul’ (Deuteronomy 6:5).”
Eusebius says: “Why did God place this commandment before the rest of the commandments, seeing that it is more demanding than those that follow it?
For someone may refrain from murder, adultery, and theft, yet not attain love for God.” The Solitary says:
“My dear friends, God placed first the very thing that causes human beings to keep the rest as well.
For if they do not remain steadfast in that first commandment—to acknowledge him as the one God—they cannot love him either.
And if they do not persevere in love for him, neither will they restrain themselves from murder and sexual immorality.
But if they draw near to acknowledging his lordship and loving him with all their heart, it is clear that they will also obey the rest of the commandments.
Through their obedience to God and their abandonment of the deeds he commanded them not to do, human beings will live at peace with one another.
The teaching of the blessed Gospel, however, does not merely restrain evil deeds.
It also puts an end to the thoughts that cause those actions. It says, ‘Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you,
and pray for those who persecute you’ (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:27). These commandments bring the inner person toward purity
of mind. But the commandment of the Law given to the people commanded that those deeds should not be expressed through the body,

while also constraining the inward thoughts so that their desire would not be carried out in action. For example: ‘If the load of your enemy’s donkey falls on the road, and you are unwilling to help him lift it,
you must certainly help him lift it.’ Here it leads a person toward a good deed, though the mind has not been purified within. Our Lord, however, purifies the mind itself through his Gospel.
He says, ‘Love your enemies.’ That is, ‘I am not merely commanding you to do good to them with your outward limbs,
but also to take up love for them within your inward senses,’ just as God loves even those who hate him. His deeds themselves bear witness to his love.
For he makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and sends down his rain on the righteous and the unrighteous (Matthew 5:45).”
Eusebius says: “What is the beginning of the inner person’s way of life?” The Solitary says: “Freedom from the love of money.”
After freeing himself from the love of money, he must necessarily free himself from the passion for praise.
Then, after this, he must live with excellence of mind, in humility and endurance, in tranquility and prudence,
in the joy of his hope, in watchfulness over good thoughts, and in perfect love for God and for other people.
Through these things he is to approach purity of soul, which is the goal of the entire way of life that God has commanded a person to follow in this life.
For all his commandments bring a person as far as clarity of soul.
But when he has struggled and overcome all the evil passions, and has become established in purity of mind, he moves beyond the entire way of life commanded by God in this life,
and from then on begins to pass from clarity of soul into the way of life of the new person, who is no longer a slave placed
under a law, but a beloved son freed from everything belonging to this world. He begins to become God's confidant, as he comes to share in communion with God through knowledge of him.
God converses with him through revelations of mysteries, as he grows in spiritual things.
This is the order of life of the inner person, whom Paul calls the spiritual person, who judges everything but is himself judged by no one (1 Corinthians 2:15).
For no one even knows him, nor is his glorious way of life visible to other people. He himself, however, judges everything.
Eusebius says: “How does he judge everything?” The Solitary says: “Listen in keeping with the aim I have set myself.
Because he is above everything visible, he understands everything, and judges and condemns whatever is not good. Little by little he rises toward perfection in the spiritual order,
so that he is judged neither by God nor by other people. Through him, however, all those below him are judged, just as the world is judged through the saints,
because, although they were like them in nature, they did not attain excellence like them in their deeds. To show that I have not said these things casually, let us turn to our Lord's teaching [?],
which makes known to us that, after a person keeps the commandments and approaches purity of soul, he becomes a member of God's household, sharing in his mysteries.
For he said: ‘Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father,
and I will love him and reveal myself to him’ (John 14:21). That is to say, after a person fulfills the commandments laid down for him—and his diligence in fulfilling them comes from love—
then I too reveal myself to him by making my mysteries known. For someone to approach a state of mind higher than clarity of soul is one of the gifts given to us in the world to come. But the one
who applies himself diligently to this way of life that I have described—God begins, even here, to give him some of the gifts to come, according to what he is capable of receiving in this life.
Thus, as I said, by freeing himself from the passion of love for money, he begins the way of life of the inner person and is led onward as far as clarity of soul.
From clarity of soul onward, he begins the way of life of the new life, growing continually in knowledge.
As for my use of the terms ‘inner person’ and ‘outer person,’ the apostle also uses these names. For he says: ‘May Christ dwell in your inner person’ (Ephesians 3:16).
And: ‘Even if our outer person is wasting away, the inner person is nevertheless being renewed day by day’ (2 Corinthians 4:16).
And: ‘I delight in God's law in the inner person’ (Romans 7:22). Now the good way of life of the outer person is this.
That he should not engage in debauchery and drunkenness, or in curses and insults, or in the desires of his flesh;
while praising God aloud with his mouth, along with other things like these. For if someone is concerned with these things alone,
he remains within the limits of visible human conduct, serving the Lord of all in the position of a slave, and like a hired worker who works for his wages.
This way of life is what the apostle calls the natural person, who does not receive spiritual things, for they are foolishness to him.
And he cannot understand, because it is discerned spiritually (1 Corinthians 2:14). Eusebius says: “How is it that he cannot perceive that it is discerned spiritually?” The Solitary says:
“I am speaking in keeping with the subject I am discussing. For everyone whose entire way of life appears good to other people,
and who practices almsgiving, fasting, and vigils that keep sleep away, has his whole mind confined within his conduct.
The joy of his hope is awakened within him by his labor. And all the glory that is prepared
for him through the abundant goodness of God in the world to come, he thinks he receives because of his deeds, and not from the treasury of God's mercy.
For this reason, if he is told about spiritual things of which he has no perception, the person speaking to him seems foolish in his eyes. For everything that people hold to in this life,
and that they consider virtues in accordance with God's will, is empty in comparison with what they will experience. For all the things here will pass away.
And God will establish human beings in another order after their resurrection.
For in the life to come they will not serve him by burning incense, or through offerings and visible deeds.
But the natural person does not know how to hear of anything beyond these visible things. For everyone who is natural in his good deeds,

if these are set aside for him through the demonstration of something greater than they are, remains as though in despair. For he has not approached the greater thing, and he has let go of what he held.

Through this he comes into a hopeless state of mind, because he has not perceived that there is anything beyond the things he expected. For this reason he does not understand that it is discerned spiritually.
And if he is told that everything he considers glorious is nothing in comparison with the things of the Spirit, he cannot accept the judgment conveyed by this knowledge.
But as for the natural person [?], if God grants him a revelation, he informs him beforehand about things that are going to happen in the world. And when a gift is given to him,
he receives the ability to perform signs, because these are the very things praised among human beings, and through them people can come to faith in God, who is invisible.

And because he works with God through his outward bodily members, God also places the gift in his bodily members, so that his tongue may declare what is going to happen, and his hand may perform a sign.
This gift is not only unremarkable, but is not even desired by a
person who has experienced spiritual revelations. For just as many ranks can be seen drawn up in their divisions before the king,
and each division surpasses the next in its clothing, the spectators stand watching: they see the first division and praise the appearance of its clothing;
the second appears, and they are still more astonished; the third division comes out, and they marvel at its clothing. From then on, the first division becomes contemptible in their eyes.

They are not despised because their clothing is contemptible; rather, the splendor of the others makes them seem contemptible. Through this illustration, understand the mystery of which I am speaking.”
That although it is a great thing for someone to have something that is going to happen in the world revealed to him, the revelation of the new life is far greater.

It is more glorious than that to the same extent that the world to come surpasses this world in which we live. But for all who have not perceived that mystery, all their sense of greatness is placed in the things before their eyes.

For the gift received by a person at the level of the soul heals bodily pains through its signs, through the faith of those who see them. Matters concerning stumbling blocks and conflicts are also revealed to him,
things that people also predict from experience of such matters, like a ship’s pilot concerning the weather at sea, or a physician concerning bodily illnesses.
But the apostles received both the power to perform signs and the wisdom of the other life, because they were chosen for the [?] of the nations:
so that through signs the mystery of Christ might be believed among them as coming from God, and through the wisdom of the future life they might teach people about their hope.
Yet in their eyes, knowing their hope was far greater than performing miracles.
For many have performed astonishing signs, cast out demons, cleansed lepers, and healed the sick, yet have not perceived the wisdom of that world.
For it is greater than anything marvelous in this world. Consider the Corinthians: while

they were performing many wonders by speaking in tongues and interpreting tongues, and through prophecies in which they foretold things that were going to happen in the world, along with other wonders,
they were not even able to hear the mystery of the wisdom concerning that world. For the apostle rebukes them and says
that it was not only when he came among them that he was unable to speak with them about the wisdom of that world, which he calls solid food,
but, he says, “Even now you are unable to receive it” (1 Corinthians 3:2). “But we speak wisdom among the mature:
wisdom not of this world” (1 Corinthians 2:6). Although they were displaying signs, they had not reached this level.
For being envious or resentful does not prevent someone from performing signs before unbelievers.
But there is no way for someone to perceive that wisdom concerning his hope unless his mind is pure. For the purpose of all signs is instruction about God.
It is not that through them either the person performing them or the person seeing them also comes to know what to understand about life after the resurrection.
For this, in its power, is more inward than the gift of signs, just as the soul is more inward than the body.

But if performing signs is greater than wisdom concerning the future life, why did he not grant the righteous the ability to perform miracles after the resurrection, instead of wisdom concerning his mysteries?
But it is clear, as I said, that the power of signs is directed only against error.
Once people have come out of error, they begin to learn the wisdom of his mysteries.
For this reason, the power of signs is like the level of the soul for human beings. For just as the soul is placed between bodily existence and spiritual existence, being unlike the body,
yet not perfected in this life like the spiritual existence of angels, so the power of signs stands between error and truth: it leads away from error
and brings closer to truth. Therefore, because the life of that world is above error, it is also above signs, since no one there needs to come out of error.
Again, a person who is at the level of the soul has a struggle with demons. Eutropius says.
For what reason? The Solitary says: Because his conduct is visible, Satan envies him for his deeds.
He begins to petition God about waging war against him, so that, if God gives him permission, he may fight against him by every means.
Eusebius says: Why, then, does he not fight against the spiritual person through apparitions? For the spiritual person’s conduct is superior to that of the person who lives on the level of the soul.
And if excellence in deeds makes Satan envious, he must be more envious of someone who lives on the level of the spirit than of someone who lives on the level of the soul.
The Solitary says: My brothers, the conduct of the spiritual person is not visible in the body among human beings.
The good things visible in him belong not to the spirit but to the soul, since he is not bodily in his actions.
But because his hidden conduct is concealed from Satan, and no one sees it except God, Satan is not filled with envy toward him.
And if he does envy him, he envies him because of the things visible in him.

Consider our Lord: although his greatness, his knowledge, and his glorious conduct were immeasurable, Satan did not approach him in an appearance meant to tempt him except at the time of his arduous fasting.
For because he could not see his spiritual conduct and his glorious knowledge of God the Father, he was not fully stirred to envy in his wickedness.
For in his outward life Christ conducted himself like other human beings. But so that Satan might have an opportunity for
tempting our Lord, he arouses the malice of his envy through toil visible in the body. As for his approach to our Lord, and the designation of slanderer and tempter,
and why he was led into the wilderness to be tempted, that is another subject. But now listen also concerning the condition of the bodily person.
For if a person does not conduct himself even according to this visible good conduct, not only is he not a servant of God, but he is a stranger to God’s entire household.
It is such a person whom the apostle calls bodily. He says, “As long as there are envy, jealousy, strife, and divisions among you,
are you not bodily and walking according to the flesh?” (1 Corinthians 3:3). These people, despite bearing Christ’s name, are slaves of sin.
Scripture, then, names three conditions among human beings: bodily, of the soul, and spiritual.
Those whose entire mind wanders among evil thoughts, if they love to carry them out, live according to the conduct of demons.
Those whose entire mind is occupied with human evils, even if they do not love to carry their impulses into effect,
are nevertheless bodily because they are still stirred by these thoughts. For this is what the apostle said: “As long as there are envy and strife among you, you are bodily.”
But if someone struggles against the evil of his thoughts and does not surrender his mind to his impulses,
and forcibly restrains himself from consenting to them, then, if he perseveres in this attitude, he is close to the level of the soul.
Eusebius says: And when does he come to live on the level of the soul? The Solitary says: When he neither does evil things nor thinks shameful thoughts. Eusebius says:
And why is someone who is not enslaved to his passions called by this name? The Solitary says: Because the nature of the soul is above evil deeds
and ugly thoughts, and it is moved to share in them because of the body, as I explained in my letter to you.
For this reason, someone who has risen above bodily things and drawn near to the order belonging to the soul’s nature is called a person of the soul.
Similarly, someone who indulges the desires of bodily nature is called a bodily person.
Listen also to another distinguishing mark: anyone who is a person of the flesh is not moved by fear of judgment.
Nor is he concerned with the wisdom that comes from instruction. When he petitions God in prayer, he has no way of gathering his mind together.
Instead, the habits and thoughts to which he is accustomed wander through his mind. He looks upon God as though he were a human image.
But someone whose mind belongs to the soul has a love of learning. With great effort, he is able to gather his mind together in prayer.
His mind remains gathered together only briefly. But it does not remain pure even for an instant. Listen to the reason.
Because his soul is occupied with distracting impulses, or with studying various subjects, or with bodily labor,
these things stir within him even at the time of prayer. He cannot look upon God with a collected mind, because his mind wanders among images that give way to one another.
Above all, this is because he has not reached the level that is higher than the life of the soul, which looks upon God in a way that transcends human thought.
But because the spiritual person is above bodily thoughts, there is no time when his entire mind is not awake to the wisdom found in God.
If someone has not experienced what I have said, let him accept even this which he has not understood on the basis of those earlier things which he has experienced. Eutropius says:
Because in conversing with you we have discovered many things that had never even entered our minds, we—my brother Eusebius here and I—were eager to come to you. For although for many years
we have been away from our own region, coming to you has benefited us far more than our remaining there.
For we have counted the practices we established for ourselves as nothing compared with this knowledge that you outlined for us in the letter to us.
What happened to Paul has happened to us as well. Just as he formerly boasted and rejoiced in his conduct under the law,
thinking that this was perfection and that there was nothing else, until he received the knowledge of Christ, so we too used to think
that what we held to was perfection, until we learned from the meaning of your words how far we fall short of perfection.
And just as the apostle, because of the surpassing greatness of knowing Christ, counted as loss those things he had formerly considered righteousness,
so we too have scorned the joy we took in our labor, so that we may boast only in our hope in God. The Solitary says:
I too, my brothers, since I perceived your good disposition, which seeks the truth and does not boast in customary observances,
have desired to speak with you about the things through which you may dwell in a place of peace, with your souls sheltered inside a wall that is not shaken by any misfortunes.
Eusebius says: We likewise ask you to explain to us the distinctions between these orders. Do not expect us to be the ones asking questions.
For we did not even know that they existed, nor did we know what to ask about them.
Instead, of your own accord, tell us whatever comes to your mind about the passions of the soul and their causes.
The Solitary says: I will begin to speak about remorse, and in which of these three orders it is found.
It is found neither in those who live according to the body nor in those who live according to the spirit: not in those who live according to the body, because of their evil disposition;
and not in those who live according to the spirit, because through joy they have risen above this feeling. Remorse is found only
in those who live according to the soul. I will also explain its cause. Because the person who lives according to the soul is moved by the fear of God, he comes to be distressed over his deeds.
From sorrow over his sins, remorse is born in him. Let us now proceed to explain weeping with tears as well: which thoughts stir it in the mind in these three orders.
As for the weeping of the person who lives according to the body, even when he weeps before God in prayer, these thoughts stir his weeping: reflection on his poverty;
the memory of his troubles; anxiety about his children; distress over those who wrong him; concern for his household; remembrance of his dead;
and other things like these. As these thoughts persist, sorrow increases within him, and from sorrow tears are born.
But these thoughts stir the weeping of the person who lives according to the soul during prayer: fear of judgment; reflection on his sins;
remembrance of God's kindnesses toward him; reflection on death; the promise of things to come; fear of being deprived of them;
and other things like these. As these thoughts persist, his mind is stirred with the emotion that brings tears.
But if other people are with him, unless he is very watchful, his weeping does not arise from these reflections.
Instead, he begins to be stirred by a passion for praise from other people.
As he considers their gathering and his own position among them, the gaze of other people stirs him to the emotion of weeping through empty praise.
But these thoughts prompt the weeping of the spiritual person: wonder at God's greatness; amazement at the depth of his wisdom; the glory of the world to come;
the waywardness of human beings; and other things like these. As these thoughts persist, he pours out tears before God.
His weeping, however, does not arise from the feeling of sorrow, but from great joy. For weeping is also born of joy, just as many people, when
they see their loved ones after a long time, shed tears from the joy of seeing them. But when the spiritual person's weeping arises from sorrow, this is its cause:
when he remembers how far human beings have gone astray. This is like our Lord's weeping when he entered Jerusalem,
and like the statement that he was grieved at the deadness of their hearts (Mark 3:5), and like what Paul said: “Now I speak about them even as I weep” (Philippians 3:18).
And again, like what is written about him in Acts: for three years he did not cease weeping (Acts 20:31).
This weeping, however, did not arise from the mind of the spirit, but from thoughts of the soul:
whether about the waywardness of human beings, or about sufferings and afflictions, or because they were pleading for help to come to them from heaven.
For the spiritual person does not readily weep, because of his constant joy. If he does weep, he is stirred by thoughts belonging to the soul, as I have said.
This is like Simon Peter, who wept bitterly when he remembered his denials of our Lord.
For wherever our Lord wept, the evangelist explained which thoughts made him weep.
That is, when he came down to the thoughts of human beings and looked at their dead hearts, he wept over them.
But when a person's mind is in the Spirit, he does not weep, just as an angel does not weep.
If weeping were part of the spiritual way of life, then the righteous would weep continually in the kingdom, because there they belong to the Spirit.

There is therefore no weeping in the spiritual way of life. What, then, is the standing of someone who weeps continually in relation to spiritual growth? He is like a newborn baby who cries continually.
And just as a newborn baby, as it advances toward full stature, ceases crying, until it reaches a stature at which crying is no longer fitting,
so too someone who continually weeps with discernment, if God grants him progress in spiritual growth, ceases weeping as his mind grows in the Spirit
and comes to be joyful. But someone who has no sorrow of mind at all and is not moved by compassion
stands in the same relation to a spiritual person as someone not yet born stands to someone fully grown in bodily stature.
For just as someone not yet born is entirely within the womb, and nothing of him is visible in this world,
so a person who has no sorrowful contrition has his whole mind confined here and does not go out in his thoughts into the other world.
Although I have already expressed this point in another letter, I felt compelled, for your benefit, to state it to you as well.
For often you do not come across that letter. What I have said concerns the cause of weeping, even when emotional sensitivity is naturally present in people.
As for the sighs that come from everyone, these distinctions between thoughts that I have described concerning weeping also stir them up.
Now I come to explain the character of love as well: what causes bring about its acquisition in bodily-minded, soul-minded, and spiritual people.
This is so that all who understand what I am saying may know how far they fall short of true love.
For I see that everyone who wishes to do so imagines that he possesses love,
even though the level of love for human beings is below the level of divine love.
Unless a person first reaches the measure of love for human beings, he does not rise to the measure of love for God.
As blessed John also said: “Someone who does not love his brother whom he sees cannot love God whom he does not see” (1 John 4:20).
I will now describe the distinctions within love and which thoughts nurture it in the soul. First, however, learn that God has placed it in us by nature.
For if the soul's capacity could not be moved by love, we would not have been told, “Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 6:5). Thus, in a person
who is bodily-minded, these passions awaken the love belonging to his nature: desire and affection.
Desire grows through thinking about the body, and love of possessions increases through love of many desirable things.
For someone who wants to be known in the world for power, honor, and grandeur is the one in whom love of wealth increases.
And affection for these things stirs his love for particular people. I mean those who possess these things.
For this reason, the love of bodily-minded people is not steadfast, because it begins to burn in their minds through things that change, and their love rests on things that do not last.
It is clear that when the things that caused their love change, their love changes along with them.
For their love begins with beauty that fades, wealth that vanishes, and authority that is dissolved.
Let us now turn to another order, those who live on the level of the soul, in whom neither true nor false love is found.
They have no false love for the reason I am about to explain. In someone whose conduct is on the level of the soul, the passion for wealth is not strong,
nor is the desire to satisfy his cravings. For this reason, no circumstance prompts him to love people, since he thirsts neither for wealth nor for the love of beauty.
Because of these things, the feeling of love does not arise easily in him. Even if he thinks he loves people with divine love, he has not yet approached this measure.
For love of God is acquired not from the bodily world, but from understanding his mysteries.
And because he has not approached this, he falls short of loving all people. For this is perfect love: to love everyone as God does.
And if someone who lives on the level of the soul loves particular people, his love comes not from knowledge, but from a circumstance that presents itself to him. But if his love is true,
and he loves those he loves with knowledge, then he will not hate someone who does him harm. But if
he does hate, let him know that just as a circumstance prompted him to hate, so a circumstance prompted him to love.
But someone whose understanding is on the level of the soul can love only someone who agrees with his teaching. Yet this too is not true love.
For true love loves even those who do not agree with one's teaching, just as God loves even those who do not agree with his will.
But the spiritual person fully possesses love for God and for people, not through preoccupation with anything visible or because of it, but from knowledge.
Eutropius says: “From what kind of knowledge?” The Solitary says: “May our Lord reveal it to you, my beloved, for the sources of his love are beyond your hearing.
Even when they are spoken of, you are not capable of understanding them. Yet I am going to speak of some of them.
“True love is acquired from serenity onward. Anyone who is below serenity has not yet reached up toward its height.
“But this gift of perfect love is given to the whole human race in the world to come.
“For every gift a person receives from serenity of soul onward is one of the gifts that follow the resurrection.
“Since no one will hate another after the resurrection, is it not clear that true love is a gift from God?
“I will also speak of another passion: the thoughts involved in jealousy in each of these orders. The bodily-minded person's jealousy concerns the following:
“The authority of others, the wealth of those richer than he is, and the lives of those who live more comfortably than he does. The whole passion of his jealousy is stirred by envy.
“His envy itself also begins with affection for these visible things.” Eusebius says: “And how could someone in this condition be freed from these things?”
The Solitary says: He could have freed himself from them through hope in the things to come.
For if he had understood the weakness of the things here and the strength of the things promised, he could have avoided being overcome by this passion.
Now that I have spoken of the cause of his pain and the means of healing it, I turn to the person of the soul, showing where his zeal comes from, what it is, and what arouses it.
Zeal begins to arise in the person of the soul for this reason: he has risen above the evil deeds that are visible in the body,
but has not become aware of things greater than himself, so he supposes that the state he has reached is perfection.
And because the rest are inferior to him in visible deeds, he begins to be stirred by zeal and to criticize their deeds.
His zeal causes him to accumulate hatred. If, however, he does not love the honors of the world, his zeal comes not from envy but from what he supposes to be righteousness.
But if he loves honor, his zeal is stirred by envy. The wretched man does not know that, just as he judges people of the body, so he himself is judged by spiritual people.

As the apostle said, he cannot understand, because it is discerned spiritually (1 Corinthians 2:14). This passion that I have described concerns someone who is at the level of the soul in his conduct.
But the zeal of someone who is at the level of the soul in his knowledge arises for this reason.
Because he has approached the study of wisdom and become caught up in a supposed understanding of various things, he looks around in his arrogance and sees everyone as beneath him.
And because he has not become aware of mysteries greater than himself, he thinks that he knows the truth.
From then on he begins to burn with zeal against those who disagree with him, supposing that they are utterly mistaken.
This is like the zeal Paul had against the disciples, because he supposed that he knew the truth and that they were mistaken.
As for the zeal of those two ranks, their thoughts extend even to killing, just as certain individuals among
the righteous were zealous for the destruction of human beings. Thus the zeal of people of the soul and people of the body is bounded by these two aims.

These are people who are at the level of the soul in wisdom and conduct, and people who are at the level of the body in mind and deeds. But in the spiritual person there is no zeal for anyone's destruction.
Our Lord was like this: not only was he not zealous in this way, but he also rebuked his disciples because they had become inflamed with zeal against the Samaritans.
Eusebius says: What does this mean, that he said to them, “You do not know what spirit you belong to” (Luke 9:55)? The Solitary says:
If they had known to what measure of wisdom he had come to bring them, they would not have seethed with anger over these thoughts.
Indeed, after they understood what knowledge they had received in the mystery of Christ, they not only rose above that way of thinking but also became perfect in love for the wicked.
But the zeal of the spiritual person—if it is right to call it zeal—is nothing other than this:
he burns with divine zeal and complete love for human beings, to bring those who have gone astray to the knowledge of the truth.
This is what our Lord and his disciples did. Understand also what I am saying here:
from the time a person begins to distance himself from evil deeds, he experiences many changes in his way of thinking. Then he approaches the level of the soul.
And when he begins again to be purified of his inner thoughts, he still has much ahead of him. Then he reaches serenity.
But from serenity onward, it is a mystery without limit. As for explaining the distinctions between these things—how a person moves away from bodily life and approaches the life of the soul,

and what distinctions there are between those who are bodily in their conduct and those who are bodily in their understanding, and between those who live at the level of the soul in their understanding
and those who live at the level of the soul in their conduct—there is much to teach about them. For just as there are many changes in the growth of the body, so
there are many changes in the growth of the mind. And just as, when someone is ten years old, his thoughts correspond to his stature,
and when he is fifteen his impulses are different, and when he is twenty still others are added,
and when he reaches the age of thirty his former concerns are replaced by others, so there are many changes in the growth of the inner mind.
And because this world is bodily, the body's stages of growth are recognizable in it. But inner growth is visible only to someone who has become separated from the body in his understanding.
And just as children grow in the womb, and their growth is not visible to those in this world, so the inner minds grow, and their growth is not visible until we enter that world.
And just as, when infants come out of their mother's womb, the bodily stature of each one becomes visible, so when we come out of this spacious womb of the earth
and appear in that world, the measure of each one's understanding is revealed, showing in what things it has grown, whether in evil or in good.
But because explaining these changes would be a lengthy task, I say that I will at least show by an illustration when a person begins to love other people.
Just as the body, when it completes the first stage of childhood and enters the second, that of youth, can no longer avoid being stirred by desire for the pleasure belonging to its world,
which is sexual union, so also in the growth of this inner person: when he completes the first stage of infancy, which is freedom from anxiety in the fear of God,
and enters the second stage, which is serenity, he cannot avoid being stirred by the pleasure belonging to his world, which is love for other people.
And just as the body in its youth stands fully within its own world, so this inner person also stands in another world through love for
other people. But if I were to tell you everything point by point, you would know that the length of our discourse would exceed the five books of the Law.
These things, however, are seeds that are to grow abundantly within you. I say this about the order of the soul, apart from the case of someone who has already become bound by the habit of his labor.

Everyone who lives at the level of the soul in his understanding is bodily in his conduct. And everyone who lives at the level of the soul in his conduct is bodily in his understanding. For the latter rejoices in his labor, while the former boasts of his wisdom.
Alongside these is another order found among human beings: nothing takes place in such a person, either inwardly or outwardly, apart from the works of the flesh.
And there is someone who has begun to leave bodily life behind but has not yet approached the life of the soul. What his experiences are is another subject.
And there is someone who has begun to rise above the life of the soul but has not reached spiritual understanding. To speak about his impulses is another matter.
Human nature cannot seek a spiritual way of life, because it is beyond nature and is given to human beings in the other world.
In this life, however, it is given by God alone to whomever he knows it is fitting to give it, as in the case of Paul, whom he brought to this measure along with the rest of the disciples.
For this reason, no one is judged for not having reached this greatness. Eusebius says.
But I think it is wrong for someone, after hearing these things, not to take the trouble to pray continually to be made worthy of them.
The Solitary said: I will now explain who those people are who give way to resentment and cannot easily be reconciled.
Although anger flares up in everyone, even these passions are not strong in those who are sluggish by nature.
But someone who wisely restrains his anger within himself is not only free of resentment, but is also
close to overcoming the passion of anger itself. But someone who restrains his anger, not out of wisdom for his own benefit, but cunningly silences it within himself—this is a resentful man.
I will also explain the cause of his resentment. Because he has not been cleansed of anger so as to be patient through a good disposition,
his anger's desire has therefore not been satisfied by blows or curses, and so his inward impulses form resentment within him for a time of revenge.

People of this kind, then, take a long time to be reconciled. Eusebius said: And who is the person who, when he becomes angry, does not hold on to resentment for long? And what causes his resentment to be less?
The Solitary said: A person whose anger is fierce and who quickly bursts into rage does not remain resentful as long as the first person I described.
Eusebius said: How so? The Solitary said: Because the impulses of his anger have found relief through an outlet in words,
his thoughts do not remain within him for long in their hidden rage. Indeed, he often even regrets his earlier actions.
Along with many other things of this kind found in godless people, who are never satisfied with harming their companions.
For I am not speaking about demons, but about human beings. Anyone who does not restrain his envy and knows nothing of reconciliation is not counted among human beings.
Rather, according to the meaning of the Gospel, he is counted among Satan's angels, since he sent them with those angels into the fiery hell.

For if they had not resembled them, he would not have condemned them along with them. God's judgment is not unjust. Let us also explain the passion of malice and what causes it to increase in the soul.
Generally speaking, it exists in everyone. But the passion of malice is strong in people who are eager to find fault with the actions of others.
Eusebius said: And how could they lessen this passion within themselves? The Solitary said: By not gratifying their minds.
Rather, when their minds stir them to wander in their thoughts, they should restrain their minds and give their hidden impulses no opportunity for an outlet in words.
For just as closing the mouth and nostrils reduces the breath that sustains a person's life,
so, by refraining from speaking about others, the inward passion subsides. And after this passion has ceased, the passion of love enters.
Their soul has no opportunity to be moved by love for other people as long as this passion barks within it. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.
Listen also to the opinion others have held about the nature of the soul. They say that it is moved by three passions,
namely, discernment, love, and anger. But their thinking about it was very inadequate, for animals too are moved by these three passions.
Animals love their young, become angry with anyone who strikes them, and have the discernment to honor affectionately the person who feeds them.
For example, dogs distinguish their masters from strangers and love them; and it says, “The ox knows its owner” (Isaiah 1:3), along with many other things like these.
For the nature of the body is moved by these three passions. The first is its natural love of life.
The other two arise from this passion that I have mentioned. For because the nature of the body is bound to the love of its own life, against anyone who threatens its life
it unleashes anger, while it singles out for honor anyone who supports this passion of love for its life. The nature of the soul, however, is certainly above these three passions.
In a human being, only the body is moved by them. As for the soul’s power of understanding, I have explained it briefly, in keeping with the aim I set myself. The end.
The second discourse: On distinguishing the passions of the soul, the cause of their movements, and which of them belong to its nature and which are outside its nature.
When we had finished the midday service and went in to him after the conclusion of prayer, he began to say to us: “My dear friends, I,
like a helpful physician who concerns himself with bodily ailments to show how they may be cured, have also taken care, according to my limited ability,
to tell you not only what you requested, but also other things about which you did not ask,
so that everyone who takes care to study these things may find in them a cure for his hidden ailments. But I know that few concern themselves with this teaching.
Nevertheless, I also explain the very cause of their neglect: why they do not concern themselves with the ailments of the soul as they concern themselves with the ailments of the body.
When they understand this cause, even those who excel in their conduct will restrain their anger,
so that they will not become angry with those who take no care for the life of their souls. For it is from lack of knowledge that the righteous become angry with sinners.
For if they knew how long it takes for a person to be found worthy to become a man of God in his deeds, they would acknowledge God’s grace,
since through his help they have advanced to this measure, and they would feel sorrow for sinners rather than the anger
of zeal. Now the reason a person concerns himself with the ailments of his body is what I will explain.

Because this whole natural world, through the activity of its elements, serves the body and not the soul, it is therefore the body that feels the comforts found in it and the afflictions that come from it.
And because its comforts and afflictions are visible in the body, a person is prompted to take care over these things.”
Eusebius said: “We have heard the reason you gave for why people concern themselves with bodily ailments.
But what is the reason they take no care over the ailments of the soul?” The Solitary said: “Because the nature of the soul is subtler than all bodily things,
and its life is awake in a life higher than the body, since even after its separation from the body it continues in the life proper to its nature,
people therefore do not see its ailments or the causes that wound it, nor are they aware of the thoughts that help to cure them.
For it is not harmed by exposure to the air, nor is it helped by a mixture of medicinal roots.
But God, who knows the causes of the soul’s injuries, which arise from evil deeds, restrained people from those very deeds by his threats,
saying: ‘You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, and you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor’ (Deuteronomy 5:17 ff.),

along with the other commands that they should not covet what belongs to one another. Thus, when they refrain from these things that take place in the body, their inward movements too will dwell in peace.”
But when human beings were in harmony neither with the good nature within them nor with the commands of the Lord of all,
because of this disobedience of theirs, they became entangled in every kind of evil. Their knowledge was changed into error, and their inner being was corrupted by defects.
And, so to speak, they could neither see nor hear, but became like the dead, without feeling any love for their inner being. While, in the indolence of this
state of mind, human beings remain, most of their impulses are directed toward the love of praise. Eusebius says:
You have explained very profoundly and truly the passions, their causes, and the healing of their defects.
For if someone takes care to understand these things, he truly becomes a man of God in his thinking.
But since your discourse has approached this passion of the love of praise, we wish to know what cause gives rise to it. The Solitary says:
This passion begins with conceit. Conceit itself begins with a foolish way of thinking, and this foolishness comes from ignorance of this life.
For human beings do not consider the frailty of their affairs or the emptiness of the praise that comes from them.
And because they do not gain understanding of the wonders of God's works, the wisdom of his providence, and the lowliness of human nature—

how, while still blossoming, they withered; while still exercising power, they were brought to nothing; while still being exalted, they were humbled; and how the condition of their nature is subject to every kind of change,
and all their affairs are subject to dissolution—and because they do not trouble to reflect on these things, they are drawn unawares into loving praise from one another.
This happens especially because a person does not stop to think and say: What is this vanity that has taken hold of me, so that being seen by human beings matters more to me than being seen by God?
I long for their approval, and not for God's approval,
as though their praise raised me to the praise of the Lord of all, and as though honor from human beings made me equal to the honor of the angels. What a wretched human being I am!
Though God created me free, I have placed myself under the mastery of many, since I am everyone's slave by flattering everyone.
As though Christ endorsed the praise of human beings! And as though
human beings constituted the court that would judge my actions! If, then, a person's mind continually dwelt on these thoughts,
the passion of loving praise would not dwell in him. For these impulses are enemies of this passion.
And just as, when many people live in a house in harmony and with one mind, their enemy cannot enter their dwelling because he fears them,
so this passion is kept away by the great harmony of these inward thoughts. But because a person's mind is empty of these impulses, he first becomes deficient in understanding.
Then he becomes conspicuous in his deeds; then arrogant; then a lover of conceit; then a lover of praise.
And from the love of praise he becomes entangled in envy. For wickedness does not give birth to envy in everyone; rather, different passions cause it in different people.
In conceited people, envy does not spring from wickedness, as others have said, but from vainglory, as Paul said:
“Do not be vainglorious, envying one another” (Galatians 5:26). But in those who have no love of praise, their envy is born of wickedness.
The cause of the growth of their envy is that they dare to look at the honor given to others.
As for craftsmen, those who hear legal cases, judges, or wise men, their envy of one another comes from the love of glory.
For because each one of them wants to be praised himself, he envies the praise given to his companion. Other people, however, envy one another out of malice.
Such are the rest of the poor: their envy of one another is not for the sake of being praised. Rather, their envy of one another concerns collecting a larger gift.
But this kind of person, who loves praise through acclaim for visible deeds, does not have much malice.
Eusebius says: Why is malice abundant in others but slight in this person? The Solitary says: Because someone who loves praise is generous with his gifts.
And because he looks to be praised by everyone, there is no room for the passion of malice in his boastful impulses. Indeed, he often even takes part in kindness.
Through the passion for kindness, the passion of malice is put to an end. His kindness, however, does not extend to everyone, for that belongs to compassion that resembles God.
Instead, his kindness is confined to those who praise him, as with judges, military commanders, and rulers who lavish their wealth on spectacles for people to see.
Their failure to give to the poor, however, comes not from malice but from their contempt for righteousness.
For, as I said, the passion of malice grows weak through the love of praise. But anyone who does not love to be praised for the arrangement of his worldly affairs,
and does not give to the poor from what he has—this kind of person has much malice in him, and because of his malice he is devoid of compassion.
But for that first class of person, who is praised in the world, the love of glory from other people becomes the reason he does not show compassion to the weak.
For because he has become enslaved to praise for material things, he does not turn toward the nobler praise that comes from generous giving.
But I will state what calls forth compassion in every person. Anyone who is not compassionate can become compassionate in this way:
by compelling his mind, even when he is unwilling, and training himself to give to those in need, so that through his constant giving abundant compassion may dwell in his soul.
Someone who has nothing with which to put an end to his malice through giving and become compassionate can become compassionate in this way:
by compelling his mind, even when he is unwilling, forgiving those who wrong him, and not being drawn into repaying evil. But the passion of anger
in this kind of person, who seeks praise for the arrangement of his affairs—when he becomes angry, his anger arises not from the malice of envy but from pride.
For pride is one thing, and vainglory is another. Arrogance accompanies pride, and haughtiness accompanies vainglory.
Furthermore, the passion that produces haughtiness is one thing, and the passion that produces arrogance is another. Hatred arises from arrogance when the arrogant person becomes angry.
From haughtiness, however, comes contempt for other people. Thus, when the mind becomes haughty, it grows angry out of contempt.
The mind of the arrogant person, however, grows angry out of hatred. When an arrogant person rebukes someone, he rebukes him out of malicious hatred.
The haughty person, however, does so because he despises people and considers them worthless. These passions, in turn, have a cause, and their cause has yet another cause.
Let us not recount them all—what they are and why they differ. For if someone knows them, he can avoid being caught by them.
And if he is caught, because he does not have foreknowledge of everything, he can easily escape from such occasions through understanding their causes.
This is the root cause of all evil occasions: what I mentioned above, that people do not recognize the weakness of their nature and the changes in their circumstances.
But because not everyone has the same attitude in loving praise, I will explain the distinctions within this passion:
If not all its distinctions, then at least three variations within it, showing how it differs from person to person.
Those, then, who love to be praised for advancing worldly affairs and to receive greetings of respectful obeisance have arrogance in their love of [?].
But those who seek to be acclaimed for good deeds are conceited in their thinking. Eusebius says: “And why, when both have the passion
for praise, do they differ from one another in these two passions, so that one is arrogant and the other conceited?
And when the same passion is active in them, why does it not make them alike in these other respects?” The Solitary says:

“They are not alike in these other passions because the cause of loving praise is not the same in someone amply endowed with authority to manage affairs and in someone who seeks to be acclaimed for good deeds.
And because their causes differ, these passions are also found in them differently. For those who hold authority have their minds puffed up by authority.
And because many people are subject to them, their minds are raised above those under their control.
And because not everyone is capable of doing the things they do through their authority and the wealth they possess, their hearts are therefore also lifted up.
But those who are acclaimed for good deeds have this passion of conceit stirring within them whenever they are seen by people who know their deeds.
For this reason our Lord, who knew the cause of their conceit—that it arises from being seen by people—commanded them to conceal their good deeds from human sight, keeping them hidden, when he said:
‘Do not practice your righteousness before people with the intention of being seen by them’ (Matthew 6:1). Now this class of people, who seek to be praised for good deeds
and seek to be honored in people’s eyes through actions considered good, are more cunning in dealing with people’s minds than the first class I mentioned.
But that first class, who seek to boast about matters concerning the advancement of the world, do not understand the wisdom of cunning; indeed, they are very ignorant about human passions.
The reason for their ignorance is this: because they are not concerned with the upkeep of cities for the sake of the duty itself, but only to be praised, their thinking is confined
to these thoughts, and they are ignorant about people’s minds.
If their authority and wealth were taken away from them, they would be no different from animals in understanding.
But those who are concerned with restoring regions and ruined places, not in order to be praised
but in order to help, have room in their thinking to become wise in other good things as well.
Now that these two classes have been discussed—how, although they are subject to the love of acclaim, they differ in other passions—I will speak about another class of people.
These are people who love to be acclaimed neither for improving the world nor for virtuous deeds, but seek to please people through authority alone.
People like this make themselves like everyone, whatever their opinions. An enemy is not easily found for them, because they speak to everyone in whatever way pleases that person’s mind.”
And they make great use of an appearance of humility in their dealings with people, just as Absalom did toward the people.
Because he wanted to gain praise through authority, he spoke to his listener with an appearance of humility, according to the aims of the listener’s mind.
But this type, who wants to win approval solely through authority, is more deeply versed in cunning deceit than the two groups I mentioned.
Now that I have spoken about their agreement in loving praise and about the different variations in their impulses, I will also say in which other passion they agree.
All three groups I mentioned, then, when they hear anything said about them that discredits them in people’s eyes, do not at first flare up in rage.
Instead, they are struck by the passion of distress, as people who have met with the opposite of what they love. Then, out of that distress, they quickly flare up in anger.
This describes the first group, which boasts in the display of possessions. But the person who, for his good deeds,
receives praise is troubled by distress more intensely than the first.
His distress leads him into hostility toward the person who criticized him. But the person who, under an appearance of humility, seeks to win people’s approval through his authority,
does not become hateful or angry when he hears that some people have spoken badly of him. Instead, his mind is overwhelmed by great distress.
These three groups of people who love praise, then, agree in feeling distress when they are criticized. But they do not agree in their other passions.
But anyone who does not love praise is filled with an impulse of rage whenever someone insults him in word or deed,
becoming hateful and abusive. For rage gives birth to cursing. Eusebius says:
“Why, when he hears that he has been spoken of badly, does the person who seeks to win approval through his authority under an appearance of humility not flare up in rage?”
The Solitary says: “Because his love of praise does not allow him to. For he seeks to win approval through the humility he displays in exercising his authority.
And he does not want to appear hot-tempered, lest he be criticized all the more.” Eusebius says:
“But look at the first group you mentioned, who seek to be praised for their possessions: they too love praise.
And when they hear something that discredits them, although they are struck by distress, they flare up in anger. Why does the passion of loving praise not restrain them
from appearing angry?” The Solitary says: “Because they do not seek to gain praise through an appearance of humility, such that appearing hot-tempered would bring them criticism.”
Eusebius says: “You have spoken very well.” The Solitary says: “I will also explain another point to you:
which of these three groups of people faces a struggle to escape the passion of loving praise, so as not to do anything to win people’s approval.
Know that those who boast in worldly display have no possibility of undertaking this struggle.” Eusebius says:
“That is contrary to their nature. For since their nature commends humility, how can they have no struggle against empty praise?”
The Solitary says: “Because their minds are captive to the things of this world, and they do not reflect on the change that human nature faces.
And because their minds are confined to what people can see, their thoughts do not leave the realm of the love of praise.”
But even that quality of their nature which praises humility has failed to become evident in them, although they praise those who are humble.
Eutropius says: “How is it that, although they praise humility, it is not seen in them?” The Solitary says:
“Because the good nature within them cannot fail to show its power, bearing witness in their minds to the beauty of kindness.
But because the passions of arrogance, pride, and love of praise have multiplied within them, the abundance of these prevents the power of their natural humility from being seen in them.
First, because a good will does not support this disposition toward humility; and second, because all the circumstances surrounding that person—
namely, authority, wealth, freedom to speak, and honor—lend their support to strengthen this passion for praise.
As a result, the power of humility ceases to fight against them and surrenders the inner faculties to the will of those passions.
The person’s own will gives these faculties to those passions as chambers in which they may dwell through their impulses.
But the disposition toward humility descends and sinks into the depths of the soul’s understanding, in keeping with its nature, so that in its own place it may show
its power by praising the excellence of humility. It reveals its inclination within the soul’s nature by commending and praising humility.
And because the person’s will has not supported the disposition toward humility by giving it a place to dwell in the members of his body,
humility is not seen in that person. Instead, the will of the body, together with all its conduct, is devoid of it.
The power of humility is hidden within that natural inclination of the soul, and it shows its power by not rejecting humility.
Yet its power is not seen in that person, because it has been driven out of him by the will of the body.” Eutropius says:
“You have spoken very forcefully. But now that you have shown that someone who loves authority cannot escape empty praise,
explain to us who it is that grieves when the passion for praise overcomes him and struggles against it so that he will not be enslaved to it.” The Solitary says:
“Someone who seeks praise for his good deeds struggles from time to time over those deeds, so that they may not be done for the sake of praise from other people.
For whenever he wants to do something good, the passion that seeks praise from other people stirs within him along with that thought. When he does the good deed, he does it for the sake of praise.

He has not yet been freed from this passion so as to do it purely, without it. But if he refrains from doing the good he has intended, he falls into a struggle, wanting to abandon the good deed he had planned.
With these thoughts, he settles on one of two things: either he completes the good deeds he wanted to do, or he prevents them from being carried out.
This, then, is the struggle into which the mind of someone engaged in good deeds falls when he wants to direct them toward pleasing God rather than other people.
But I advise someone in this condition not to neglect
doing what is good, even when his good deeds are directed toward other people’s approval.
For no one benefits from the abandonment of good deeds, but everyone is helped by their performance.” Eusebius says:
“And why does this person who wants to do good deeds have a struggle against the passion for empty praise?” The Solitary says:
For his mind occupies an intermediate position, looking both to the promises and to other people. And in order to find mercy at the judgment, he seeks to do good to those in need.
And because he is not perfect in love for other people, so as to do good to them out of love for them, his mind rejoices in being praised by them.
And because he fears the judgment, when his mind makes him aware that he does not do his good deeds sincerely, without seeking people's praise, he falls into struggle and distress.
But I, my beloved, did not wish merely to describe these passions—what they are, what they are like, and what causes them to grow—
but also their cure: I have shown, as far as I could, by what thoughts each one of them is healed.
But because many things lie before our eyes, I refrain from speaking about them. For we cannot recount all the causes of each individual passion:
what they are, what causes them to be stirred up in people, how they develop, and what impulses sustain them.
For there would be much to say about people's differing opinions and the views that many have held about them.
Some have regarded the passions as natural, holding that the cause of their strength lies in nature itself, in the way the body's constitution is composed.
Others have attributed them to the evil that has become mixed with nature. Others have called them demons
that lodge in the inner person and, they say, gain strength in a person more than they do through other causes. Some hold
that these passions belong to the soul, and that the soul itself is their cause. But to argue against each one of these opinions—
this is not the aim we have set ourselves: to determine who has spoken better than another, or whether they have all departed equally from the truth.
There are also other matters about which we have not yet spoken: simplicity, the intermediate state, and the excellence of higher knowledge.
Simplicity, because many people live in innocence; and the intermediate state, because many neither remain in innocence nor have attained higher knowledge.
Instead, they are in an intermediate position: they are far from innocence, but have not attained higher wisdom.
Most of the world belongs to this intermediate rank. They neither walk in innocence nor conduct their lives with simplicity.
Nor have they risen to spiritual wisdom, so that through knowledge they might become excellent in complete simplicity.
Rather, this entire intermediate rank is deceitful in its conduct, evil in its deeds, and cunning in its thoughts, along with all the other hateful qualities.
But I say that it is very beneficial for a person, if he is not advancing toward excellent wisdom, not to abandon the first rank of innocence.

Otherwise, by abandoning his original simplicity without attaining glorious knowledge, he may find himself in the intermediate rank, which conducts itself entirely through the inventiveness of cunning schemes.
For just as, if someone leaves his house to go to the city but does not enter the city, it would have been better for him not to have left his house than to remain on the road,
so it is more beneficial for a person to be innocent without knowledge than to abandon innocence without approaching the wisdom that enables him, through knowledge, to live in complete simplicity.
True innocence, however, is found in knowledge. For there is no innocence without knowledge that does not have
foolishness mixed into it. For when this knowledge, which is higher than ordinary innocence and than the whole intermediate state of cunning schemes, is perfected in a person,
On what our Lord said: “Be innocent as doves and shrewd as snakes” (Matthew 10:16).
Eusebius says: “What sort of people are those who stand in the middle rank?” The Solitary says:
“Judges, those who hear lawsuits, and those engaged in disputes, if they do not advance toward virtue.” Eusebius says:
“How can a person have the snake’s cunning?” The Solitary says: “Our Lord gave us the following meaning through the example of the snake’s cunning:
“Just as the snake knows that it cannot shed its old skin in a spacious place, but only when it forces itself into a confined place and narrow crevices,
“and then, as it stretches its body, squeezes itself under pressure, and struggles to get out, its old skin gets caught between the crevices,
“and it comes out renewed, leaving its skin behind, so also with us, through training in afflictions and the toil of mental endurance,
“the inner person will strip off all the conduct of the old person. Then, when it has stripped off everything old, its departure from the body will be in complete purity.
“But let us also leave aside another category about which there was more to say. Most people are eager to recount the bad things about others, but do not recount their good qualities.
“When someone hears many good things about a person, they do not stay in his mind, nor does it occur to him to recount them. But if he hears one disgraceful thing about him,
“there he is, rushing and eager to recount it to everyone he meets, even without being asked.
“As for the good things, even when asked, he is reluctant to recount them. And those things that contain
“benefit for their hearers he keeps silent about, while he recounts what harms everyone who hears it.” Eusebius says:
“What shall we say about such people? There is great evil in them, and it leaves no room for goodness to take hold in them.
“Yet we see that there are virtuous people who take pleasure in speaking of others’ good qualities, while they do not even want to hear anything that brings disgrace on them.”
The Solitary says: “The causes of these things are not bodily temperaments alone, nor do these things arise solely from evil.
“Some people have become accustomed to them through the habits of their upbringing. In some, they arise from a lack of training in good things.
“Some, because they have no concern to keep people from stumbling, do not conceal reports that disgrace them. In some, they arise from a lack of care for their own souls.”
Eusebius says: “If that capacity for care is in them, why have they not taken care?” The Solitary says: “The capacity for care is indeed implanted in all human beings.

“But each person cares about what he loves and what first took hold of him. For no one lacks the capacity to care about whatever he wants to care about. And so that you may know that causes outside us

“are what stir up these passions within us, consider a man who is captive to vainglory because of his wealth and authority. If his wealth and authority are taken from him, that passion of his also ceases.
“This passion no longer lives in him. Rather, the presence of his authority stirred it up in him, and the removal of that authority put it to sleep in him.” Eusebius says:
“Do these passions belong by nature to the soul or to the body, and are they stirred up in a person by various causes?
“But since there are wise people who have distinguished which belong to the body and which belong
“to the soul, I want to be assured whether they have spoken truthfully, or, if there is something better than their account, to grasp it in my soul.” The Solitary says:
Distinguish those they have assigned to the body from those they have assigned to the soul. Eusebius said, “Those of the body are sleep and hunger,
thirst, desire, and debauchery. Those of the soul are anger, jealousy, conceit, envy, love of power, pride, boasting, and affection.”
The Solitary said, “Those of the body are indeed as you have said. But these passions do not belong to the soul by nature.
Rather, because of the things to which the body is bound by its need for them and its love of them, a place is made for these passions in the mind.
For tell me, where does envy come from? Is it not from a person loving something and seeing someone else surpassing him in it—
that is, in wealth, power, beauty, skill, or being known to important people?
Everyone who loves something and sees someone else honored for it envies him. As for power itself, or wealth, skill, beauty, or being known to important people,
what has caused these things to be loved and envied: the body’s need for them, or the soul’s need?”
Eusebius said, “The body’s need. For the soul has no need of wealth, bodily beauty, or power.
For what benefit does the soul’s nature receive from a person ruling over other people? Even power itself is manifested through the body.” The Solitary said,
“If the body’s need for these things has made them objects of love, it follows that love for these things has become the cause of envy in whoever loves them.”
Eusebius said, “If love for these things is the cause of these passions, how do they gain power over the soul? For, as you have said, they are foreign to its nature.
And if they have no affinity with the soul, how has something foreign to the soul’s nature gained power over it?” The Solitary said,
“Just as blemishes and wounds arise in the body from an external cause.” Eusebius said, “They do not arise outside it. Rather, it is injured by something that strikes its nature.”
The Solitary said, “Even if it is wounded by something that strikes its nature, those scars are nevertheless foreign to its healthy condition,
since they can disappear at any time. Again, when someone turns to sleep, he sees images that are outside him,
and although they are not within him, fear of them gains power over him because he has turned toward them. But when he wakes and turns away from them to awareness of himself,
