as time passes, those images gradually disappear from his memory, his fear of them is removed, and he returns to his former state,
so that he neither remembers them nor fears them. In the same way, when the soul’s nature turns toward the body,
the harmful influence of the body’s passions and impulses gains power over it, although they do not exist in the soul’s own nature.
But when someone turns his attention away from the body toward his soul, and does not turn toward the body’s desires for a long time,
turning instead toward his soul through good deeds, these passions gradually come to an end, and he stands in the serene condition of his nature.” Eusebius said,
“You have given a very helpful illustration of this kind. But since you have maintained that things and the body are the cause of these passions,
we see that the order of demons neither needs our things nor is clothed in a body. Yet although it is free of these things, by these passions,
which are evil, it is stirred: by envy, wickedness, and love of power.” The Solitary said, “Although speaking about the nature of demons is quite another subject,
But since you have brought them forward as an illustration of souls, show me among them those who desire what is good and praise good deeds, as there are among human beings.
Eusebius says: Indeed, those human beings whose souls are by nature free from these passions conduct themselves well. The Solitary says:
Even if they do not do good deeds, all human nature nevertheless praises good deeds. In this the soul’s noble power is recognized: it praises what is good.
But because human beings are bound by love for their bodies’ desires, they prevent the goodness of their nature from being seen in them.
Among the race of demons, however, you have not shown me even one who praises good deeds, so that I might be persuaded by the nature of demons regarding your illustration of souls.
For the whole nature of souls is in accord with good things, in that it praises good deeds, just as the entire will of demons is in accord with evil.
Eusebius says: If the nature of demons is not accepted as an illustration of souls—that it is not the body that causes them to be stirred by these passions,
but that they incline toward them by their own nature—I will offer the example of angels.
For when the angel Gabriel was sent by God’s command to Zechariah the priest, he displayed the passion of jealousy and anger.
For he became angry because the priest’s mind doubted the promise conveyed by his words, and he showed jealousy through the punishment he imposed on his mouth. The Solitary says:

This statement that he was jealous and became angry—were these things said about him while he was in the order of his own nature and remained in his own world, or when he came to our world and appeared in our likeness?
If it was when he came to our world and appeared in our likeness that he was said to have done these things, then you should not attribute
to the order of his nature something that resulted from his activity. For if, because he became angry and jealous, you supposed that these passions belong to his nature,
then the composite sounds heard from the composite form also belong to him by nature. But if the likeness in which he appeared is ours and not that of his own nature,

and the voice with which he spoke belongs to our nature and not to his spiritual being, then the passion of jealousy that he displayed to Zechariah in response to his doubt is also a passion belonging to us, not to him.
The blessed apostle, however, attributed these passions not to the nature of the soul, but to the body.
For he says in the Letter to the Galatians: “The fruits of the flesh are sexual immorality, impurity, indecency, sorcery, hostility,
quarreling, jealousy, anger, contentiousness, divisions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelry, and everything like these” (Galatians 5:19ff.).
And if these are its fruits, and he did not include among them love or humility or kindness or any of the good passions,
to whom, then, should we consider these praiseworthy passions of love and virtue to belong? If to the body, they are not present in it apart from the soul’s good will.
For when the soul turns away from the body toward virtue, it makes its virtue shine forth visibly in the body’s conduct.
And if they do not belong to the soul by nature, what is the cause of those good passions? Eusebius says:
And are there two wills in a human being? The Solitary says: There is one belonging to the body and another belonging to the soul.
Otherwise, which will does God blame through the prophet when he says of the people of Israel, “They followed the will of their own hearts” (Jeremiah 9:13)?
For the noble nature within them praises good deeds. And blessed Paul said to the Galatians:
“So that you do not do whatever you want” (Gal. 5:17). If there is only one will in our nature, then it is no longer possible for us to will
not to do what we want. And which will is it that wills within us that we should not do what we want?
Rather, he urges us to put an end to the will of the body, and, through the good will of the soul that is within us, not to carry out the will of the body.
For you should know this: if the soul has an inclination toward these evil passions by nature, then they belong to its nature.
And if they belong to its nature, then it will not cease to be stirred by them, even after its departure from the body.
For just as the body sleeps because sleep belongs to its nature, and eats because it is hungry by nature, and drinks because it is thirsty by nature,
and these things are always present in it, so too the soul would always be inclined toward these passions if they were in its nature.
And if they belonged to its nature, a person would not be blamed for doing something that belongs to his nature. For just as a person is not blamed for sleeping,
because sleep belongs to his nature, nor for eating, because hunger belongs to his nature, nor for joining in sexual union,
because desire belongs to his nature, so too, if he were envious or proud, he would not be condemned in judgment for having these things in him, because they belong to his nature.
But the fact that these passions are condemned by God, that he constantly commands that they should not exist, and that he imposes punishment on anyone who submits to them—

these things, together with the others I mentioned above, show that the soul’s nature is free from these passions, and that through causes outside the body and within the body they gain power over the mind.
We also see that these passions stir not only in human beings, but also in other bodies that have no soul.
For we find that the nature of animals, birds, crawling creatures, and fish in the sea is stirred by six passions:
anger, malice, affection, desire, discernment, and pride.
For birds have discernment according to their nature, and affection for the companionship of members of their own kind.
And we find malice in animals and crawling creatures. The canine species is prone to anger and has discernment.
For a dog barks angrily at strangers and knows to honor its masters more than strangers. And among mares we find that they walk proudly.
Now these passions are not stirred in these bodies because of a soul, for their soul is only their blood,
and they do not possess the higher nature of the soul. But if you wish to distinguish the passions, we find three divisions in the human being:
one belonging to the nature of the soul, another to its activity through the body, and one belonging to the body itself.
To the nature of the soul belong knowledge and divine love. To the activity of the soul in the body belong good deeds.
For good conduct belongs to the soul’s activity in this life, because the nature of the soul is higher even than good conduct.
For good deeds are performed through the body: compassion for the weak, chastity, holiness, and the rest of virtue.
For if good deeds belonged to the nature of the soul, and not to its activity in the body, how is it that those good deeds cease in the new life?
For the way of life in the new life is higher than chastity, giving to the poor, renunciation, and endurance of afflictions.
It is also higher than refraining from wrongdoing and becoming defenders of the needy and bearers of their burdens. Yet these are the deeds we are required to do in this life.
But when our body is transformed at the resurrection, we will be raised above these deeds as well, so that instead of a way of life based on deeds, we will have a way of life based on knowledge.
Again, we find that there is rivalry over evil and rivalry over good.
“Do not envy one another,” he says (Gal. 5:26). And again he says, “It is good to be zealous for good things” (Gal. 4:18). This,
however, is good rivalry. Which of these two kinds of rivalry do we consider to belong to the soul's nature?
For its spiritual nature is higher even than being zealous for good things. Rather, being zealous for good things belongs to the soul's [?].
And so that you may know that the soul's nature, in the depth of its understanding, is hidden from the body's members, while through its activity in the body it is moved through the body's senses,
observe that when one of the internal organs, the brain, or the heart is damaged, it is not the soul's nature that has been damaged, but its activity in those organs.
For when a part of a lyre or a musical pipe is damaged, it is not the finger that plays it that has been damaged.
Rather, the exercise of the finger's skill has been prevented from making itself known through the instruments, the lyre or the pipe.
And because those instruments through which the skill could be heard have been damaged, the hand's activity in them has also fallen silent,

although neither has the hand lost its skill nor has the hand itself been damaged. In the same way, the soul's knowledge is preserved in its nature, while its activity works through the body's members.
For if the soul's very nature were revealed in the body, one could also speak without forming words. Eusebius says:
“Yet these virtues of the soul—love, affection, humility, gentleness, compassion, and mercy—are not seen in everyone.”
The Solitary says: “They are present in all human beings, and there is no one who does not love and praise them.
“But the power of their action is not seen in some people because of the many causes that hinder this virtuous activity from appearing in the body.
“For when the sun shines, if there are thick clouds and mists in the air, they prevent its light from being visible to us. In the same way, habits
“and the bad upbringing in which a person is raised prevent the virtue of the soul from being visible in that person's life.
“And just as, when the clouds and mists are swept away, the sun's radiance is fully visible on the earth,
“so, if bad habits are removed from a person, all the soul's virtue is readily visible in that person.
“And just as the higher the sun rises in the sky, the smaller the shadows of physical objects become through its powerful light,
“so, the more the soul is revealed in the body through its virtue, the more the shadows of mistaken thoughts fade through the light of its glorious understanding.
“Therefore, my beloved, let us ask God at all times to make the light of his knowledge shine within us, so that we may see the virtues he placed within us when he created our soul.
“And as far as you are able, my beloved, do not neglect the labor of learning. For if there is no knowledge, our whole inner being is darkness.”
Through study, our mind too is gathered back into itself. And because recounting them benefits you, I will tell you stories about various people.
There was a certain wise man who, so that nothing would interrupt his study, gave up living inside the city and built himself a cell outside its wall.
Beside it was a plot of land sown with wheat, and he constantly passed by it.
When someone from his city asked him whether its crop had sprouted, he said, “I do not even know whether it has been sown.”
See how beneficial the love of study is to the soul: through its constant occupation with study, it does not allow the mind to wander away from it.
I myself have actually seen a man who lived among two hundred people.
Because he did not allow his mind to wander, as the account about him says, more than twelve years passed without his knowing
who stood beside him in the row. Another wise man remained undisturbed when there was an uproar in his city. Someone said to him,
“How is it that everyone is disturbed, while you are calm?” He replied, “How many times have I seen an uproar like this even in a dream!
Those who are disturbed have good reason to be disturbed, because they think they are awake. But I am in a world of dreams, and what I see is a dream rather than reality.”
The man who had questioned him answered, “Then you ought to be disturbed because you are dreaming, since dreams disturb everyone.” He answered,
“I would be disturbed if I did not know that I was dreaming. For people are disturbed only because they think that what they see in the world is real.
And a person is disturbed in his dreams only because he thinks that what he sees is real. But the true awakening of the resurrection is coming,
“and everyone will realize that his life in the world was like a dream.” A certain man, when he was maliciously insulted and called ‘black-faced,’ was not upset, but picked up a mirror.
As he looked into it, one of those standing there asked him, “Why are you looking into it?” He said,
“If my face really is as the man insulting me said, I have no right to be angry, because he spoke the truth.
But if what he said is not true, I should not be upset, because I am not as he said, and a thing does not change to match the name it is given.”
When a certain judge was told, “People call you Death,” he answered, “If only I could show no partiality!”
A certain well-known man had been trying for ten years to persuade someone under his authority about a matter,
but the man would not be persuaded. As he still patiently persisted with kindness, one of his friends said to him,
“I am amazed that you have not become angry with him, since he has not listened to you despite all this time spent persuading him.”
The man said to him, “Do not be amazed at me for being patient with him.
For more than fifty years God has been urging me through his commandments to obey him, and I have still not obeyed him and done his will. Yet in his kindness he has put up with me.
If I have not listened to God, are you surprised that a human being has not listened to me, or that I have been patient for ten years without becoming angry with a human being like myself?”

One of the holy men was struck hard enough to break his leg. When another man saw that he was not angry with the one who had struck him, he said to him, “How is it that you did not become angry when he inflicted such a severe injury on you?”
That holy man said to him, “Even if I had been walking along the road, how often something like this would have happened to me through stumbling over a stone!
Even now I consider it as though there had been a stone in my way and I had stumbled over it unintentionally.”
A certain solitary’s disciple broke the vessel from which he used to drink. The disciple thought he would be angry with him, because he had no other vessel, but he said to his disciple:
“Do not be distressed about this, for it was not something unbreakable that broke. It had always been destined for this.”
A certain soldier had grown old in military service, and another, younger than he, was honored by being given a place above him in the ranks. When people saw that he was neither angry nor envious,
he said to those who marveled at him, “Even if his body stands above me, my mind can still be above him.
Look: even the palace wall stands above all of us, and we do not envy it. So let us not be envious over bodily things.
But if one of us surpasses another in wisdom, let us be jealous of that—not so that we hate him, but so that we strive to rival him.”
Another soldier was boasting before a philosopher that he had spent years in military service. The philosopher said to him, “As a soldier,
you have years behind you. But how long have you been wise?” One of the brothers told one of the holy men that he had been in the clergy for forty years.
He said to him, “I too have seen a man who had been called a merchant for forty years, yet he could not get his daily bread without borrowing.”
Another man boasted that no meat had entered his mouth for thirty years. That blessed man said to him:
“It has been thirty years since meat entered your mouth. How long has it been since a curse came out of your mouth? You have observed for thirty years something that was not commanded.
But have you observed, even for a week, what you were commanded with every warning?” A certain blessed man lived among many brothers,
and had spent many years in his monastic life. When someone who was his junior in discipleship received clothes finer than his,
and his brothers told him, “So-and-so received clothes better than yours,” he said, “The one who received them is also a member of my body.
Just as, if the right hand is covered and the left is bare, the bare hand is not angry with the clothed one, so we ought not to be distressed or envious at the comfort of others.
For if I had received them, he would necessarily have suffered hardship. And if our Lord accepted suffering for our relief, are we seeking a comfort that causes hardship to others?”
A certain wise man was robbed of his possessions, yet remained without anger and made no demand for restitution. The man who robbed him said to him, “Why are you not angry with me?”
He answered him, “I regarded you as death. When death strips everyone of their possessions, no one is angry with it.”
Now, my beloved, because of the simplicity of these brothers of ours who raised objections, since they did not fully understand what was said earlier,
and so that we might not wrong their good intentions, I wished to enrich their understanding through accounts
of the sayings related about these men. May God grant all of us that our souls may be trained in every virtue. To him be glory forever. Amen.
Here ends the second discourse, on distinguishing the passions of the soul, on the cause of their movements, and on which of them belong to its nature and which are outside its nature.
Again: the third discourse.
On another occasion, when we went in to him and prayed, he began to say to us: “My dear friends, do not grow weary of hearing these words repeated.
Rather, because I want you to understand them clearly, I am compelled to repeat the point, urging you, my dear friends, to understand this:
Anyone who is at or below the level of serenity of soul has neither true love that does not stumble nor the joy that dawns in the spirit, which is not perceived by the body,
but is hidden in the understanding of the mind. Nor does he have any means of experiencing knowledge of the mysteries of the world to come,
except through great labor and the bearing of many burdens, first desiring to be cleansed of these passions. For these passions, my dear friends, are the blindness of the mind.
Serenity of soul, however, is the light of its knowledge. For merely hearing names does not give a person knowledge of their mystery.
This applies not only to spiritual mystery, but also to the names used in other kinds of wisdom. For everyone hears the names of medicinal roots,
and that some are hot and others cold; but no one knows the properties of the roots bearing these names except someone who has studied medicine.
Likewise, in the wisdom of the Chaldeans, the names of stars and the zodiacal signs of the regions are mentioned. Yet not everyone who hears them knows, merely by hearing, the mystery of these names.
So too with this wisdom of Christ: we know only its name. For we have heard the man so rich in the beauties
of wisdom, Paul, say concerning God the Father, ‘In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge’ (Colossians 2:3). We hear the names of the treasures,
but we do not know their mystery. When someone says ‘the treasures of the world to come,’ he has not thereby said what they are.
Again, when Paul, rich in knowledge, said, ‘We speak wisdom among the mature,’
and specified, ‘Wisdom not of this world’ (1 Corinthians 2:6), he said that it exists, but did not explain what it is like or in what mysteries it consists.
Nor, when he said that we receive knowledge, did he say what that knowledge itself is, or in what mysteries it dawns,

so that the listener might suppose from these statements that, when the discourse turns toward the world to come and speaks about it, merely hearing words about it also gives him knowledge of what they mean.
But if a person is at or above the level of serenity of soul, he can not only understand the words of the new life, but also becomes close to God through the revelation of mysteries.

For when his understanding rises to the level of serenity and above, Christ reveals himself to him. But to anyone who is at or below the level of serenity, Christ does not reveal himself in the knowledge of him.
As I showed above through the testimony of the Gospel: ‘Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father,
and I will love him and reveal myself to him’ (John 14:21). This is the road that brings one near to God. This is the path along which a person travels toward Christ.
For the very mystery of Christ, which is to be revealed to the saints in the new world—and which is their way of life after the resurrection—
is at the level of serenity of soul and above. This way of life is a mind that shares in communion with God through knowledge of him.
For this reason, a person cannot receive the revelation of Christ in this life unless he obeys his commandments. It is through obedience to his commandments that there is
purity of understanding. And if anyone doubts these things, all humanity bears witness to them.
For to which of all those whose minds are confused, troubled, and [?], and whose deeds are evil, has Christ revealed himself through knowledge of his mystery?”
And who has taken care to submit himself to the law of Christ in complete humility of mind, without his mind being illuminated by hope in God?
And who has taken care to cleanse his mind of evil things, without his soul rejoicing in God?
But if someone applies himself to the labor of learning, he can learn many things from people who have received a gift from God.
Eutropius says: Yet there are many who labor in ascetic practices but lack the wisdom of understanding.
The Solitary says: And what is more excellent than this—that they have cast off bodily desires?
For if they are also cleansed of inward passions, they are truly filled with joy through the good expectation of their hope.
And since you have brought me to this subject, I want to explain in my discourse what this practice of labor is, and what causes it to arise in each person.
First, however, know that this labor is neither bodily nor of the soul. It is not bodily because it does not deal with the evils of the body.
And it is not of the soul because it does not put an end to inward passions. Nor does the nature of the soul engage in these labors.
Now that I have explained its character, listen to what causes it. This labor, then, consists of standing on one's feet and keeping one's eyes awake;
going barefoot without shoes; abstaining from food; and other forms of self-affliction. These things arise not from knowledge but from fervor of mind.
This fervor begins to arise in the mind because grace has granted it the awareness that there is another hope.
And because of fear of the torment of hell, a person begins to despise these things and to love the things that have been promised. And for this reason
his mind grows fervent to afflict his body. He afflicts his body because of these thoughts that I am describing.
For when he reflects on the torment to come, he seeks to escape that torment through the affliction of his body here.
This labor, however, is sustained not by knowledge but by the fervor of his love. If his fervor happens to subside, he begins to slacken in his labor.
But if fervor has been stripped from his mind and he has not changed his labor, he no longer endures his labor out of love,
but because of people's reproaches and a timid anxiety about breaking his rule.
This labor is commendable to bodily people, but contemptible to people of the soul. Spiritual people, however, welcome everything that is done in the name of Christ.
In the same way, our Lord Jesus Christ himself extended a hand of hope to every weakness through the reward he promised for everything done in his name.
But I will explain why it is great in the eyes of those whose minds are bodily, and contemptible in the eyes of those whose wisdom is of the soul.
For anyone whose thinking is bodily knows nothing beyond what can be seen in the body.
And because he sees the body being afflicted by something in which he himself finds comfort, he marvels at the man who labors.
And because that man despises the things he himself loves, he thinks that this is the height of righteousness.
For this reason, bodily labor appears righteous in people's eyes. For the Pharisees too were like this.
Because they set themselves apart from the people by distinctive clothing and footwear, together with prescribed fasting, they were considered righteous in the eyes of the people.
But our Lord, to expose their inner condition, which did not agree with their outward appearance, said, “You are those who justify themselves in the eyes of others.
But God knows what is in hearts, for what is exalted among human beings is detestable before God” (Luke 16:15). Your outward appearance, he says, through which you appear to others
as righteous—God does not look at the outside as human beings do, but examines what is within.
And because he sees that your hearts are not pure before him, even that which makes you great in the eyes of others is detestable before him.
But people whose wisdom belongs to the soul despise bodily labor for this reason:
because their minds are trained in learning, through the wisdom of their own conceit they look down on outward labor.
But the spiritual person, because his whole mind is absorbed in God, becomes like God.
And because he knows each person according to that person's measure, his mind accepts all the differences among people and praises them.
And because those two orders, the bodily and the soulful, are below serenity, they are the ones who find fault and make accusations.
They make themselves judges of everyone's deeds, and, so to speak, nothing pleases them except what their own minds desire.
The reason that only what their own minds desire seems good to them is this: they suppose that what they hold to is the righteousness and wisdom of everything.
Eutropius says: “Since you have said several times that anyone whose mind is at the level of serenity or below
does not understand when he hears the mystery of the other world, we want you to explain to us why he does not understand.”
The Solitary says: “Pay attention, my dear friends: the true birth of our true self is above serenity.
For even baptism itself, which was appointed as a symbol of that new birth after the resurrection, is above purity.
And that true birth of the resurrection, in turn, is above purity.
But so that you may understand fully, pay attention to what I say. Consider baptism, resurrection, and serenity—for their mystery is one—
as resembling a birth sac. Just as the beginning of a person's bodily birth consists in coming out of the birth sac and entering the way of this life,
so the complete birth of our true self consists not in remaining confined to purity alone, but in coming out of serenity and entering the knowledge of the life of that world.
And just as the birth sac serves the infant as an intermediate stage between life in the womb and life in this world, so that it may come out of the birth sac and enter this life,

so serenity serves our hidden self as an intermediate stage between the good conduct of this life [?], so that it may come out of serenity and enter the true life of that understanding which knows the spiritual world.
And just as a person cannot perceive or see the colors of this creation unless he has first been born from his birth sac,
so a person cannot perceive and understand the mystery of the spiritual world unless he has first been purified of every defilement, left behind purity of deeds, and entered the life of knowledge.
And because only a few have been found worthy, through divine help, to be purified of the defilement of evil things, for this reason only a few have perceived the wisdom of the new world.”
But now I will rise in my discourse to a lofty subject and encompass much in a few words. From serenity onward, then, there is another life, the life after the resurrection.
It is the way of life of the new human being, not through deeds but through knowledge. For in that life good deeds stand below purity.
Purity of mind is the limit of the entire power of natural and written law. Beyond purity, however, the way of life is spiritual.
It is called spiritual, however, not because it has been fully perfected by the Spirit here. For this is not granted apart from the new world.
Rather, it is called spiritual because it is moved by knowledge that is higher than the order of the soul established in the body. For in true spirituality no one
has lived since the world was created, except Jesus Christ our Lord alone. Eusebius says: What, then, was the manner of life of the righteous people of old?
The Solitary says: They conducted themselves in the righteousness of good deeds, while all their righteousness extended as far as purity of mind, and no further.
For even the natural law established within them had no power to do anything else except teach the mind to distinguish between good and evil.
For even God, when he recounts good deeds in Ezekiel, does not call the person who accomplishes them spiritual.
Rather, he says, “The person who does these things is righteous” (Ezekiel 18:9). For nowhere did the Old Testament call a human being spiritual.
For human beings cannot rise above purity of mind in this life unless a person receives a divine revelation.
For how can he manage to break through the barriers that stand between him and purity?
By barriers I mean evil deeds, hateful passions, and impure thoughts, which stand like barriers before a person's mind.
And how much less can he manage to break through them and pass beyond them into a true vision of that world?
For one person breaks through the barrier of sexual immorality, yet malice remains a barrier before his mind.
Another breaks through the barrier of the love of money, yet envy stands like a barrier before his understanding, along with other things that we will not recount in full.
But for a person to break through each and every one of them and emerge beyond them all—I do not think his nature is capable of this without God's help.
But if he breaks through them all and passes beyond them, he has left the way of life of this world and begun the way of life of that world.
Its way of life is the true vision of its mysteries. But Jesus our Lord
began to live above purity of mind in his glorious conduct. For none of our passions turned him toward the sight of our world.
The sight of our world is love for it. And never did a barrier of hateful thought stand before his mind.
For he himself broke down the barrier of all hostility, as Paul said: “He broke down the barrier of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14).
Eusebius says: What is the barrier of hostility? The Solitary says: Listen in keeping with the subject we have set out to discuss.
I call the whole hateful way of life composed of evil passions a barrier. It is called hostility because through this very way of life we become enemies of God.
“You were formerly enemies,” he says, “through your evil deeds” (compare Colossians 1:21). And because, just as a barrier obstructs bodily sight,
to see anything beyond it, so evil conduct obstructs the soul’s sight from seeing the mystery of that world. Eusebius says.
And why did blessed Paul not say that he demolished the barrier of hostility, but that he breached it? The Solitary says. In another manuscript it is written as follows.

This is said about the hostility between the Jewish people and the nations, which was abolished through Christ. As for the rest, I will satisfy you concerning the point you asked about. He did not say that he demolished it,
because this hateful way of life had long been firmly established throughout human nature, and no one had been able to breach it and pass beyond it into a new way of life.
But when our Lord was born in our world, this barrier of evil conduct could not stand against him.
Instead, he breached it by the power of his knowledge and was beyond it from the beginning of his birth.
Through the breach he revealed in it, he gave human beings hope that they would pass beyond it after the resurrection. Through the breach he made in it, he shone light into our world from
the light of that world, which is the hope of God. Now the way of life of Jesus our Life-giver was not merely above purity,
but above the two kinds of knowledge that are above purity, which is the threefold state [?], that precise mystery of the spirit.
For he alone overcame the world by the power of his knowledge.
All the righteous, however, grew in their virtues below the level of purity of mind until the coming of Christ. But after his coming,
God gave certain individuals wisdom that illuminates the spiritual purpose, just as John the Baptist was brought up in the wisdom of the mystery of Christ.
For the life of his hidden inner person was being nurtured in the mystery of Christ. His outward way of life, however, followed the Law, in the manner of the Nazirites.
For it says, “John came to you in the way of righteousness” (Matthew 21:32), “neither eating bread nor drinking wine” (Luke 7:33).
But people whose thinking is fleshly, when they see someone whose conduct is admirable and who refrains from evil, or who stands firm in bodily exertion,
suppose that he is spiritual. Yet not only do these things fail to make him spiritual; he is not spiritual even if he has no filthy thought at all—
something that cannot happen among human beings. For when he has been purified of these things, he is still called a person of the soul.
And because he has turned toward the soul’s good way of life, he is called a person of the soul.
For the study of wisdom with a pure mind is the activity proper to the soul’s nature in this life, because it is the soul that bears these things.
For just as the body’s nature bears vigils, standing, and exhausting labor, and it is the body that suffers through them, so the soul’s nature bears the pursuit of wisdom with a pure mind.

And because the inner person shares in the exertion of the outer person, since it was the inner person that consented to these things, and the outer person shares in the inner person, since it is the inner person’s instrument,
they therefore share in one recompense. But if we call someone a spiritual person because of good deeds and a pure mind, what, then, is he to become in that world?

If he is to be spiritual, then, according to what many say, he is already spiritual in this life as well. But if he has not been perfected here, it is clear that here he is a person of the soul, and in the end he is destined to become spiritual.
Remember that I have told you several times that the spiritual way of life does not consist of good deeds
or thoughts about good things, but is an understanding that shares in God through knowledge of his mysteries.
For see, the life that human beings receive from God after their resurrection is above good works.
For there we will not be occupied with works: giving to the poor, clothing the naked, welcoming strangers, or honoring our parents;
or refraining from hatred and envy, or people thinking well of one another, or being humble and merciful, and so on.
For these things are praiseworthy and excellent in this life. Humility is excellent in comparison with haughtiness, and meekness in comparison with pride.
Rather, the way of life of each one of us there will be in a mind awakened to the wisdom of God. And because no one has risen to the exact understanding of spiritual knowledge,
no one in this world has therefore reached the perfection of being a spiritual human being, except only our Lord Jesus Christ, who showed us this mystery in his own person.
For he alone is the true reality. The apostle calls him the body and us the members (Ephesians 5:30). Eusebius says:
Why does he call Christ the body and the saints his members? The Solitary says: Because the body possesses all the abilities—to see, hear, touch, walk, and so on.
For this reason he calls Christ the body, to show that he is perfect in all the mysteries of truth. As for believers,
he calls them members, to teach that just as each individual member does not possess the fullness of the whole body,
but each member has its own particular gift—the ears have hearing, the eyes sight, the tongue speech, the hands touch,
the feet walking, and the nostrils smell—so each of the saints has been given one gift from the mystery of truth.

Christ, however, like the body, is complete in all of them. For it is with this meaning that he addresses the Corinthians: “You are the body of Christ, and members in your respective places” (1 Corinthians 12:27).
He means: Although his gifts are among you, each one of you, like a member in its own place, has one gift. For God appointed apostles in his church, after them prophets,
and after them teachers, and so on (1 Corinthians 12:28). Surely, he says, not all these are found in one person! Rather, each one of you has one, while all of them are found in Christ.
Although this explanation is very good, it is still not spiritual but belongs to the soul. For a bodily person thinks of it in bodily terms when Paul says “body,”
and a body takes shape in his mind. But a person of the soul understands it as I have said, in the sense in which the apostle also spoke of it.
But if someone were to say what Christ’s reality is, he would approach spiritual knowledge. For he did not say what it is like, but that it exists.
And when he said that Christ is complete in all truth, he did not thereby explain what his reality is. For this is something that Christ alone knows,
and that will also be revealed to the saints in the new birth of that world. For not even Paul himself, that spiritual man, would have had the mental ability to express it, had he wished,
because the natural workings of his soul in this life could not conceive the exact reality of this mystery. Eusebius says:
And what difference is there between the life of the soul and the life of the spirit? Or is perhaps something spiritual mixed into the nature
of the soul, so that when a person reaches it, he is called spiritual, while when he remains within the nature of his soul, he is called a person of the soul? The Solitary says:
There is a difference between the life of the soul and the life of the spirit just as there is a difference between the life of the soul and the life of the body.
Yet bodily life is not a different nature apart from the body, nor is spiritual life a different nature apart from the soul.
But when someone turns toward the desires of the body and carries out its passionate impulses in deeds, he stands at the bodily level.
But when someone turns away from the body and fulfills the activity of the soul within him through good deeds, he is called a person of the soul, because in his deeds he has turned toward the soul.
This is just as he is called bodily when he turns toward the body in his actions. But because the soul’s nature itself is spiritual,
and the proper order of its nature is not the performance of deeds but spiritual knowledge, if someone rises in his knowledge above the performance of good deeds,
he is no longer at the level of the soul but at the spiritual level, because he has turned toward knowledge of his soul’s nature,
which is spiritual, yet is called “of the soul” because it is clothed in the body and is moved through the body’s own senses. This, then, is how these terms are distinguished.

For this reason, my beloved, only isolated individuals, if it is right to say so, have approached the spiritual way of life; a few have approached the way of the soul; and the whole world follows the bodily way.
The spiritual person lives in joy and divine love. The person of the soul performs his deeds in fear and pride, unless he is humble by nature.

He is anxious not to become lax in the observances prescribed for him. This is the reason why the passion of pride gains power over him: he does not know that there is a hidden way of life that is not visible in the outward limbs,
through which he might learn his own deficiency in comparison with what is hidden. He therefore comes to imagine that perfection
is his. And because he sees people living in a bodily way, he comes to think that he is better than they are.
For this reason, true humility, which comes from knowledge, is found only in a spiritual person. Our Lord, who was perfect in the spiritual way of life, said:
“Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). Again I say that the soul which has become aware of its hope is tranquil in complete humility.
And because of its humility and its great compassion, it is continually sorrowful—not with the sorrow of the world, but in the sense in which our Lord said:
“Foxes have dens, and the birds of the sky have shelters, but the Son of Man has nowhere to rest his head” (Luke 9:58).
For when the soul looks toward its hope, considers human beings, and sees where it is, it is distressed.
And again, that person reflects within himself: “Will I really have joy after my soul is separated from the body, or will I still be in distress?
And what if I am still without knowledge?” This is the sorrow that brings weeping. With thoughts like these, the soul cannot boast about anything,
but continually remains in a state of humility and sorrow. Yet joy is hidden within its sorrow, and from time to time that joy is revealed in its mind.
I am astonished at people who have not approached this measure of knowledge: how can they think that they are humble?
For the person of the soul is proud of his way of life and his wisdom. “You have told me about his way of life.” I have described not only his passion,
but also the very cause through which it settles within him. Now listen concerning his wisdom: why his knowledge makes him proud. It is because all his wisdom comes from study and instruction.
Everything he knows can be expressed in words. He does not grow through spiritual revelations that cannot be expressed, so that from their greatness he might learn
the limits of his knowledge: although he has become aware that they exist, he cannot in the same way know what they are like.
For this reason, he takes pride in everything he knows, because he thinks that he has come to know the truth.
For it is like a man who, out of his wealth, has acquired clothing of goat hair, uses silver vessels, and exercises his authority over a small number of slaves:
if he considers only what he possesses to be wealth and does not see the treasures of others, he becomes proud of his wealth, exalting himself above others.
But if he sees the wealth of others who are greater than he is, his constant remembrance of their wealth makes his own wealth diminish in his eyes.
But if he looks only at those who have less than he does, he is constantly proud. So too, someone whose knowledge is slight:
if he does not encounter abundant knowledge or see spiritual revelations within himself, the passion of pride gains control over him through his supposition that he knows something.
He is like the rest of those who, if they can interpret one prophet, become proud of their wisdom, as though they had reached the limit of knowledge in interpreting all the prophets.
They do not realize that, if they looked to higher knowledge, many things were spoken in the Scriptures that God would not have wished to be said if human beings had conducted themselves righteously.
But because error gained control over them through evil deeds, many things were spoken to put an end to error.

For example: “You shall not worship any image or any likeness” (Exodus 20:4). And likewise: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, that every soul shall worship me.” For if they had been worshiping him, this would not have been said.
And likewise: “Turn aside and know that I am who I am” (Psalm 46:11). For if they had not been looking toward idols, he would not have exhorted them to this.
Along with other things: “Love the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 6:5). For if they had been living in love for him, this would not
have been written down. And likewise, again, most of the prophets spoke of captivity, return, and the sword of the nations.
For if human beings had walked in righteousness, none of the things that were spoken of and happened in the time of the prophets would have happened.
Nor would they have been spoken of, but rather something more glorious than these. And according to the conduct of human beings, so he fashioned his teaching for them.
Many sayings of the prophets, then, were spoken to put an end to hateful things.
For, after all, to whom did God speak: to the wise and those who do good, or to fools and those who do evil?
If he spoke to fools and those who do evil, it is clear that he gave them teaching that would put an end to their foolishness and wickedness.
But the mystery of the New Testament is mightier than that of the Old. It is mightier in its riches just as the sea, in the abundance of its waves, is mightier than a small lake.
So then, following the words of the many who have no concern for the wisdom of truth or for knowing great things,
shall we abandon the hope that the Holy Being has prepared for us and occupy our thoughts with what was spoken to put an end to idols?
Why, then, do we remain at these levels and not strive to rise toward that to which Christ our teacher directed our gaze,
he who is the beginning of our kingdom, in whom we are freed from subjection to foreign powers through the enduring rule of his sole kingship?
But people who do not love wisdom, if someone exhorts them, “Approach without fear the mystery of truth and the teaching about the world to come,”
begin to be afraid, saying, “Let us not investigate or inquire, lest we go astray.” Yet in their search for wealth, look how they burrow into the earth!
Look how they plunge into the sea! They do not think, “We might die or drown.” Rather, the love of gold makes them expose themselves to every danger.
But if we had love for the truth, we would plead unceasingly with God,
that he would reveal his hidden wisdom in us. He also states another reason concerning the passion of pride:
how a person may avoid becoming proud in his mind through the study of wisdom. What keeps him from being proud is that he burns with a love of learning,
not about one thing but about many. Through this love, the passion of pride is restrained by the fervor with which the mind seeks to learn many things.
Now that you have heard the cause of these passions, and how difficult the power of humility is for the minds of people of the body and of the soul,
hear how it is found in the spiritual person, in his conduct and in his knowledge. In his conduct, it comes from what I am about to explain.
Because he has become aware of humanity’s hope and of the glory prepared for them by God’s grace, he marvels at God’s mercy.
He becomes someone who honors people with love, since he considers God’s love for humanity and the greatness they have in his sight.
But those who have not become aware of the riches reserved for humanity in the new birth become haters of people through their contempt for them.
For suppose there are people who enjoy abundant wealth and the honor of authority in their own city, but go to another city, where they have an ordinary appearance and the belongings of poor people.
All those who are unaware of their greatness cannot honor them with love, but look down on them with arrogance.
But if some who are aware of the greatness of their authority see them, clearly they cannot exalt themselves over them. Instead, they show them love with zealous respect.
In the same way as in this illustration, people hate one another in their wickedness and exalt themselves over one another in their error,
because they are unaware of the exalted glory they have through God’s grace. But whoever is aware of their honor there is, in all
humility, disposed toward other people. For he does not look at their poor appearance here, but at the greatness of their glory there.
Even if he sees them engaging in every kind of evil, he cannot hate them or despise them.
For he knows that if people were aware of what God is going to give them, they would not provoke him to anger by their wickedness.
With this understanding, then, this admirable man cannot think himself better than they are,
because he knows that they are destined to have a mind that does not conceive of sin, and that they are being kept for a life shining with the wisdom of truth.
As for the spiritual person’s knowledge, and why he is not proud through imagining himself wise, understand from a few words what I am saying.
For his knowledge grows through a mystery that is higher than the things of the body and of the soul.
He perceives this mystery through revelation, yet his natural powers of thought cannot encompass its reality within his soul. Rather, that mystery is higher than thought.
His knowing that it is higher comes from revelation. But his inability to think about it as it was revealed to him comes from the weakness of his soul, which is bound to the body.
Through these things, wonder at the depth of God’s wisdom continually reigns within him: how far this life falls short of the mystery to come,
and how human nature cannot attain these things apart from God’s grace. Therefore, as he reflects on these thoughts, he is filled with humility.

Consider, my dear friends, these three orders that I have described according to the measure of my understanding, and the reason that draws you toward love for God and for other people, which I wished to make fully known to you.
For if you become aware of the hope awaiting you, you are freed from all harmful passions,
and you establish an image of love for other people in your souls. And as I said above,
I say that those who have become aware of humanity’s hope embrace people with a disposition of perfect goodness.
For suppose there are people in a village, afflicted by crushing poverty, and a king sends them a wonderful promise:
he wishes them to live with him in his palace, in glory and honor. Those who have become aware of this promise can no longer feel hatred toward these poor people,
but even those whom they formerly despised they embrace with entirely humble love.
But those who do not know this secret message sent by the king not only fail to honor them, but look upon them with utter contempt.
Such, then, is the situation of people in this world, amid hardships and distress.
But God, in his mercy and the abundance of his grace, has made known to people in the holy Gospel the assurance of great promises.
Those who have become aware of God’s promises to humanity embrace people with perfect love.
But those who have not come to understand the mystery of humanity’s hope in the Lord of all look upon people as ordinary and become filled with hatred because of their deeds.
For we should not look at their sins here, but at the fact that they will be without sins in the future. This applies especially to people who have been baptized.
For we should regard every baptized person not as he is in this life, but as he will be in that life, and look not at his deeds here, but at his way of life there.
Eutropius says: Since you in your kindness have said that those who have become aware of humanity’s hope cannot hate or despise people,
we see that all members of the church hear the promises of the Gospel, yet few are found who do not hate or despise their neighbors.
The Solitary says: Although God’s promise has been revealed to everyone, yet
not everyone has perceived it with an understanding of what it concerns. It is like a rich man promising little children who are still babbling
that he will give them asbestos cloth, scarlet garments, and silk. Although they have heard the names, they do not know the color and appearance of the things named,
so that they might rejoice in the man’s promises and love him. In the same way, God has also promised people the great treasures of his kingdom.
Everyone hears the names themselves, but their understanding falls short of the full meaning of those names.
As the apostle said: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not comparable to the glory that is to be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).
The apostle said this while marveling at the meaning of that future greatness. People, however, have perceived only the name he gave it.
They do not understand what the mystery of that glory itself is. And because they know only the names of the promises,
they do not marvel at God’s riches, nor have they perceived the beauty of his promises, so that their minds might burn with fervor and they might love him, even if only for his gift.
And they also despise one another because they do not know their hope. Therefore, take care to understand the hope that is to come, and you will become masters of your passions.
Let your minds be occupied with these things, my beloved, for these are the things that benefit your lives.
For this wisdom brings you closer to God than the wisdom of the ages.
For all the punishments that have come upon human beings came because they were not masters of their evil passions.
What, then, do we understand to have been the reason why the people in Noah’s days were drowned in the waters of the flood?
Was it because they did not know the courses of the stars, or because they did not rule over their unruly impulses?
And for what reason was the entire settlement of the Sodomites consumed by fire? Was it because they were not skilled in disputation concerning the mystery
of Chaldean learning, or because they did not put an end to the impure desire of their hearts? For I have not found it written,
“Blessed are those who are skilled in the art of argumentative twists,” but rather, “Blessed are those whose way is blameless.”
For all the turmoil in which people find themselves through evil comes not from ignorance of things, but from their neglect of their evil passions.
For if everyone took care to understand their own passions, the whole inhabited world would rejoice in joyful peace.
For this is what benefits a person: to attend to their passions before everything else. After purifying themselves of them, it is fitting for them to pursue the study of every kind of wisdom.
For just as it is not fitting for someone whose body is stricken with disease and whose limbs are full of festering ulcers to undertake the learning of crafts,
but they must first attend to the treatment of their ulcers, and then, after becoming healthy, it is fitting for them to learn any kind of work,
so it does not benefit a person to undertake the study of heresies unless they have first taken care to learn about their passions.
And when they have become strong in the health of their soul, then it is fitting for them to learn about everything. Now one of the eastern brothers, whose name was Mara of Amida,
since he had come in just then and had not heard what had been said in the preceding days, said when he heard these things, “A person needs to learn what they do not know.
For who does not know the passions of their own soul? Everyone knows what is good for them and what is bad for them.” The Solitary said,
“If, then, my brother, your knowledge of the passions of your soul is complete, explain to me what I ask. Tell me about your hidden inner life.
I am not speaking about the nature of your soul. For you are not condemned if you do not know how to show that it exists in you, or when and how, or why and what it is. Rather, I am asking about that
which God himself commanded you to know. That is, since God placed in your nature a law that loves good things and hates evil things,
what are the causes that have made you fail to be in harmony with the good things of your nature?
And why, when the nature of your soul is not bodily, does your mind love bodily things? And which passion takes up residence in you first?
And which comes second, after desire? And which one gives rise in you to fear of the world? And which ones follow it? And what is the cause that makes them increase?
And by what means are they removed from the soul? And why do malice, envy, and sadness persist in human beings more than the rest of the passions?
For someone may have been freed from the love of money without having been cleansed of envy. And which thoughts have the power to overcome each one of these passions?
And which impulses are capable of putting an end to envy? And which are those that counter malice?
And which are those that counter fear? For just as medical knowledge recognizes particular medicines for each bodily illness,
and not every one of them is healed by a mixture of the same kind of medicinal roots, so the wisdom of the mind recognizes the thoughts that overcome each of the soul’s passions.
Again I ask: how long does each of these passions hold the soul once care is taken to put an end to them?
And when someone begins to struggle against them, why is it not easy for him to defeat them and gain the victory?
And what causes you to doubt yourself, since you yourself have not consented to them in your thoughts?
Though you hate them, they dwell in you; though you rebuke them, they do not leave; and though you plead for an end to them, they are not driven out.
Instead, they persist in you against your will. Is your conduct not a matter of your own will? And if you have control through your will, tell me why something dwells in you that you do not
want. And explain to me why a thought within you overcomes you, along with other things like these. Do not be deceived, our dear friend, by the opinion you have of yourself.
For look: when you are sick, you do not choose to think that you are healthy, as you have supposed in your simplicity that you are wise.
Oh, the ignorance of human beings! Things hidden in the depths of the soul seem simple to them.
For what is truly more excellent and powerful than for someone to understand his evil passions and subject them to the authority of his will?
For this reason, in his blessings and in the exhortations of the Scriptures, God continually praises the disposition that is diligent in seeking purity of mind.
For this alone is the true wisdom that God has placed in human nature in this life, containing neither false notions nor cunning devices.
Rather, all the Scriptures and the whole of human nature, through the natural law placed within human beings, testify that it is true. And it is this wisdom that benefits people through good works,
as Paul, the true teacher, says. But all the other forms of wisdom are mixed with cunning devices and false notions.
One must marvel at people’s error: although knowledge of the soul’s passions is powerful, everyone thinks he has no need to learn how to set his own soul right.
And if those of the school of Hippocrates, who were outstanding in the art of medicine, said concerning knowledge of the body, “Life is short, and the art is long,”
meaning that a person’s entire lifetime, however long he lives, is too short for his mind to grasp the learning contained in the rich variety of medicine,

and if, in relation to knowledge of this body with which we are clothed, a person’s life is too short to understand its constitution, together with the variety of its illnesses and what brings about their healing,
do we really dare to suppose, concerning the movements of our hidden nature, that we know the order of its changing passions? And do we suppose that it is knowledge
of an ordinary kind for someone to understand how to free his soul from evil passions?
For truly, unless divine help is openly given to a person, he cannot attain serenity of soul.
And what is to be given to us through divine action in the new birth—that we shall be there with a pure mind—
We consider it a naive idea that a person should reach this degree while still in the body.
But I heard a man of God, who was also remarkably well trained in philosophical wisdom, say:
“I do not regard any branch of wisdom as comparable to knowing how to free oneself from evil passions.”
He also said, “In my eyes, someone who drives an evil passion out of himself is greater than someone who drives a whole army of demons out of a possessed person.
For God does not judge a person who has demons in him on their account. But someone in whom evil passions dwell is subject to God's judgment because he has not freed himself from them.
For a demon must depart at some point. Its harm is directed against the body, not against the nature of the soul. But an evil passion remains in the soul after a person's death.”
I myself have also seen a man who had performed many miraculous signs. Yet he was very foolish in his thinking, since he habitually gave way to anger and curses.
Although he drove demons out of others by a prayer learned from pagans in India, he paid no attention to his own passions.
This man of remarkable wisdom, whom I mentioned above, also said, “From the time when I first turned my mind toward learning,
my concern has been to know what is good for me and what is bad for me, and I am still deficient in this wisdom.”
See what this man said about himself! Yet foolish people imagine that they have attained knowledge by putting on the monastic habit and reading books.

But so that we do not disappoint this brother's desire, I will offer him a remedy of instruction for his passions. These passions, my brother, become thoroughly weakened if a person does not do what they want.
For just as lions are strong by nature, yet through inactivity their fierce temper becomes weak, even though it remains in them,
so, by disregarding the desires of our passions, the strength of their evil becomes weak. And just as, through provocation and constant feeding,
lions grow stronger in their might, so a person who does what his thoughts desire provokes them to become still stronger against him.
But someone who becomes zealous about driving them out of himself, condemning them and expelling them from his mind, will no longer have them dwelling in his mind as masters.
Even if they pass along the road of his heart like travelers, they readily disappear as soon as he rebukes them.
For just as servants driven out of their master's house no longer have the freedom to enter as they used to,
so these passions lose their freedom within the soul by remaining outside it. A person's mind then becomes peaceful in continual stillness.
But what shall we say about others who, when thoughts multiply against them, instead of occupying themselves with reading so that a good word may quiet their minds from the turmoil of thoughts,
imagine that through much talking or attending to various tasks they can give their hearts rest from the weariness caused by their thoughts?
Do not imagine, my fellow human being, that by occupying yourself with various affairs you can find comfort for your mind, or that by engaging in them you will overcome your thoughts.
For earthly thoughts cannot put an end to thoughts of the flesh.
Even if involvement in various affairs gives you a little relief from the evil thought that troubles your mind, do not imagine that it is defeated by your occupation with them.
As for its continually stirring within you, know from this that you have not put an end to it by gaining victory over it.
Therefore, when disturbing impulses arise in our minds, let us not seek comforting help from anything visible.
For there is no power in contemplating visible things that would allow us to think we can use them to put an end to the impulses of sorrow in our souls.
Rather, let us seek help from Christ, for meditation on him is powerful and sufficient to overcome all the impulses stirred up by the disordered will of the body.
For when the blessed Paul wished to teach that through petitioning Christ we can receive strength to help us in our afflictions, he said:
“Let us therefore approach the throne of his grace with confidence, and receive mercy and find grace to help us in a time of distress” (Hebrews 4:16).
God, who alone is holy, in whose holiness the worlds of glory take pride—
may he grant us reverently to receive into our souls awe at his greatness. To him be glory forever. Amen. The end.
Again: The Fourth Discourse
On the next occasion, after we had prayed, we began to say to him: You have stored up good treasures in our souls.
Through the conversation we had with Your Excellence, we praised and thanked the one who gave you this entire gift.
But because we wish to hear about another point, so that we do not consider the terms used for virtue in a confused way,
we wish to learn the meaning of each one of them, both bodily and spiritually.
For if we hear how they differ, our minds will be more fully enlightened about the many distinctions that exist within virtue.
For when we hear about humility or compassion, we wish to know
whether humility has only one form, or whether there are different forms of compassion, just as there are different forms of sorrow.
For there is worldly sorrow, and there is sorrow for God's sake. There are also other things we have to ask about. The Solitary said:
Gladly ask about the things on your minds. As far as our limited ability allows, we will satisfy your minds.
Set out the terms you wish to ask about. Eusebius said: We are asking about fear and sorrow;
about suffering and mourning; about poverty; about compassion; about peace and tranquility; about purity; about fasting; about
service; about sacrifices; about the offering; about the altar; about hovering; about the church; about the priesthood; about love; about affection;
about consolation; about joy; about the worship of God; about the race of righteousness; about standing; about imprisonment; about bonds;
about release; about falling; about rising; about wakefulness; about sleep; about closeness to God; about fellowship with him;
about patience; about endurance; about modesty; about virginity; about chastity; about holiness; about prayer; about stillness;
about sickness; about health; about kingship; about lordship; about humility; about exaltation; about laughter; about distress; about slackness;
about despondency; about combat; about athletic training; about victory; about defeat; about weapons; about war; about trade.
On treasure. On wealth. On loss. On need. On courage. On wastefulness. On greed. On confidence.
On freedom. We ask you to tell us about these things: what the force of their meaning is in the soul and in the body, respectively.
For fasting of the body is not the same as fasting of the soul. Nor are the body's possessions also those of the soul. Nor is the body's joy the same as the spirit's joy.
Nor is the body's wakefulness the same as the soul's wakefulness. Nor is slavery in the world the same as slavery to sin.
But because these terms are used alike in spoken language, explain their meaning to us, so that we may understand them without confusion in everything of which they are spoken.
The Solitary says: Keep these terms in mind, and ask about each one of them. Eusebius says: I ask about the feeling of fear: from
what cause does this feeling arise? Does it belong to the body or to the soul? If it belongs to the body alone, how is the fear of God found in human beings, when it is absent from animals?
And if it belongs to the soul, how does a person fear hostile forces, when the soul is stronger than those hostile forces?
And because both the fear of God and worldly fear are called by this same term, fear, explain to us the different meanings of this term, fear. The Solitary says:
Worldly fear arises because of the body: that is, fear of the night, anxiety and alarm caused by circumstances, and fear of hostile forces.
The body is the cause of these fears, because it is subject to these things. But as long as the soul is in the body, it shares in the body's fear,
although fear does not belong to its nature, because it is beyond harm. Fear arises only because our nature is subject to all kinds of harm.
For just as someone who is subject to one stronger than himself fears him, but does not fear a man who is not stronger than himself,
so the body, because it is subject to everything in this world, is under the world's fear.
But because the soul's nature is not subject to any harm, it is above worldly fear. If, however, fear belongs to the soul,

we see that animals and creeping creatures, and all the rest of what is without a soul, tremble and fear whatever harms them. But the soul's nature is free from the seasons and the changes of the seasons,
from lack of food, from an abundance of crops, from the damage caused by hail, from insufficient rain, from the biting cold of the air,
from the absence of dew, from persistent snow, from the freezing of ice, from scorching heat, from the distress of pain, from the torment of hunger,
from loss of speech, from blindness of the eyes, from lameness of the feet, from paralysis of the hands, from dizziness of the head, from
[?] of the nostrils, from blockage of the throat, from bodily defects, from the blemishes of leprosy, from damage to the lungs,
from pain in the internal organs, from enlargement of the spleen, from inflammation of the liver, from an overflow of bile, from pain in the intestines,
from the torment of depression, from distress in the kidneys, from swelling of the stomach, from slackening of the sinews, from heaviness of the bones,
from damage to the arteries, from an excess of blood, from the pain of [?], from heaviness of the head, from the accumulation of fluid, from the burning of feverish chills,
from many internal ailments along with other external ones, from the wasting of old age, from failing strength, from a bent posture,
from the weakening of the limbs, from various diseases, from the torment of fever, from the convulsions of epilepsy, from burns and sores.
From the decay and wasting of the body; from foul smells; from bad news; from turbulent wars; from disturbances in one region after another.
From upheaval in one city after another; from the gloom of darkness; from the sound of thunder; from the sight of lightning; from injury by wild beasts.
From the power of demons; from the harm done by evil spirits; from the terror of dreams; from the dominion of the rulers of this world.
The soul's nature is free from all these things, while the body's nature is subject to them all. Apart from these things, there is no fear of the world.
Why, then, have I recounted all these things, except to show the emptiness of love for the body? For people love what is subject to these things, with all these masters set over it.
And when the time comes for them to be released from the body—although their release from it lets them escape all these harms—look how they grieve, how distressed they are, how they sigh!
Yet no one turns with love and joy toward the soul, which is secure against all these adversities. Just as they grieve over the body's subjection to all these things, they ought to rejoice
in their hidden person, which is above them all. The soul's nature is not only free from these things; it also has no need of the help found in creation.
For it receives no benefit from the dawning of light, nor from the rest of sleep, nor from the possession of wealth,
nor from the authority of rank, nor from the comfort of food, nor from a pleasant fragrance, nor from entertaining music.
How, then, can we place a nature that is not under the world's power under fear of the world?
But when the soul does not look toward the body, while it remains in the body and turns toward what belongs to itself, its fear is this: fear of error, dread of ignorance.
But when it turns toward the body, and it and the body are united in a single outlook, this is the fear a person has toward the world:
dread and fear of those very harms I have recounted. But when soul and body agree in a single outlook, their fear toward God is this: fear of judgment,
dread of punishment, trembling at the torment of Gehenna, fear of provoking God to anger.
But when, through knowledge, the soul becomes stronger than the body, its fear is this: that it may not be found worthy of the greatness to come,
that it may be deprived of that true wisdom, that it may be a stranger to the mysteries of God.
This is the distinction between the feelings designated by the word ‘fear.’ Eusebius says: ‘You have spoken richly and splendidly.’
‘And I do not think anyone has spoken more helpfully and intelligently about this life than you have.’ The Solitary says:
‘Write down those terms you listed and give them to me. I will speak about them one by one, as I am able.’ Eusebius says: ‘We have heard the distinctions concerning fear.’
‘But now take those terms and speak to us about them.’ On sadness. The Solitary says: ‘Bodily sadness concerns visible things.’
‘But sadness over the anger provoked by sins is a good disposition in which the soul's knowledge participates.’
‘But sadness that is not mixed with the outlook of the flesh, and instead awakens through the movements of knowledge, occurs when someone becomes aware of the greatness to come,
considers what sort of creation he is in, and contemplates the glorious nature of the soul, grieving over the feeble body in which it is confined.’ On the feeling of mourning.
‘When the feeling of mourning concerns worldly matters, it is bodily. But when it concerns sins and transgressions, it is a disposition that turns toward its hope.’
As for the humility of the inner person, it is excellence in knowledge. On poverty. Poverty of the body is being stripped of possessions and a diminished soundness of the senses.
Poverty in possessions is external to the body, but poverty in the soundness of its members is within its nature. The soul’s poverty with respect to the world,
is being emptied of evil thoughts. Being emptied of evil thoughts, however, is the wealth of its knowledge.
But the poverty of its nature in this life is a deficiency of knowledge, a lack of understanding, and limited discernment.
On emptying. Bodily emptying is the abandonment of possessions. Emptying of the soul is the stripping away of passions.
Spiritual emptying is the cessation of conjectures. Here we empty ourselves of possessions, and we can also empty ourselves of passions.
But being emptied of conjectures belongs to the life after the resurrection. On compassion. Bodily compassion is for a person to give
alms, help the weak, feed the hungry, clothe the naked, relieve the distressed, and so on.
Compassion of the soul is for a person to have mercy on those who wrong him, forgive his enemies, show kindness to those who mistreat him, and do good to his persecutors.
Spiritual compassion is to have mercy on those who have gone astray, teach those who lack understanding, bring the hesitant to firm conviction,
those who are far away into closeness to God, strangers into familiarity with his mysteries, and the lost into being found, and to proclaim hope to those without hope.
This is spiritual compassion, which is carried out in action toward the inner person. This is the demonstration of God’s compassion toward the human race.
On reconciliation. Bodily reconciliation is for a person to have a word of reconciliation for someone angry with him.
Reconciliation of the soul, accomplished within the soul, is for a person to be reconciled from the heart, in the simplicity of peace, without deceitful speech or concealed anger. On peace.
Bodily peace is the cessation of wars, tranquility in the lands, submission without rebellion, no struggle for supremacy, no plundering of possessions,
no quarrelsome disputes, no accusations in court, freedom from slander, no controversy over faith, and harmony undisturbed by conflict.
Peace of the soul is a heart untroubled by thoughts, a mind not divided over its reflections,
a will that does not quarrel with itself, calm thought that does not disturb the heart, and restfulness of soul without confused impulses.
Spiritual peace is an intellect that does not doubt the truth, a soul not confused by conjectures, the harmony of the worlds, their perfection in truth, and their movements in truth.
This peace belongs to the life after the resurrection. On purity. Purity of the body is washing away dirt, cleanliness
of the members, clean clothing, and a pleasant fragrance. Purity of the soul is being cleared of bodily wantonness,
cleansing from the defilement of filthy thoughts, purity of thoughts, clarity of reflections, and soundness of impulses.
Spiritual purity is rising above the world, no remembrance of its affairs, meditation on God, and a constant gaze upon him.
Purity like this belongs to the life after the resurrection. On fasting.
Fasting of the body is hunger through abstaining from food, refraining from meals, and growing lean through the loss of fat.
The fast of the soul: to hunger and thirst for righteousness and to abstain from evil conduct.
The spiritual fast: to abstain from recalling evil deeds, from dwelling on them, and from remembering hateful things.
But this state, in which hateful things do not enter our memory, belongs to the life after the resurrection.
On service. The service of the body: fulfilling its desires, seeking possessions, and loving wealth.
The service of the soul: seeking life, loving instruction, finding wisdom, turning away from the body, and caring for the soul.
Bodily service directed toward God consists of vows and offerings, according to the custom of the law of Israel, who practiced bodily service.
The soul’s service directed toward God: sorrowful singing and pure thoughts in a clear mind.
Spiritual service directed toward God: wonder at God, praise arising from the depths of understanding for the greatness of his wisdom:
for this is beyond the power of this life and is reserved for us in the life after the resurrection. On sacrifices and offerings.
A bodily offering: to offer God something external to oneself. An offering of the soul: for a person to offer his very self
to God through the sacrifice of his body. A spiritual offering: the mystery of communion with God,
and to offer continually in prayer pure thoughts whose movements bear wonder at God. On the altar.
The bodily altar is that representation of the people’s table on which the dead bodies of animals were laid.
The hidden altar of the soul: the mind that bears upon itself reconciliation with God through good deeds, in remembrance of Christ’s sacrifice.
The spiritual altar: the understanding that rises above the remembrance of the world and, in its knowledge, honors wonder at God. On the fan.
