The bodily fan is something the hand holds to fan with, after the example of Abraham, who drove away the birds to keep them from settling on the divided limbs.
The fan of the soul: the mind holding a good meditation with which to drive filthy thoughts out of the mind.
The spiritual fan: the understanding that flutters with movements of wonder at God. On the church.
The visible church of our world: a multitude of people, the gathering of the people, their crowding together.
But the true church: unity of thought, agreement of mind in one faith. The church in heaven (Hebrews 12:23), concerning the assemblies on high.
It is not because they dwell in places and come together in gatherings that they are called a church.
Rather, their true church is the knowledge of the truth, through which they delight in divine mysteries. On priestly service.
Priestly service is bodily when someone serves as a priest in a particular place and location, dealing with bodily things according to the law of Israel’s priests.
But the priesthood accomplished in the soul is when the mind offers pure thoughts to God in pure supplication.
On love and affection. The love of bodily beings for one another: possession of the body together with everything belonging to the body.
The love that people of the soul have for one another is the discipline of learning, the practice of wisdom.
The love that spiritual people have for one another is divine love, the greatness of their praise, knowledge concerning their hope.
If someone loves God because of visible things, his love is bodily. But if someone loves him because of the promises, his love is of the soul.
But if someone loves God alone, without any reason outside God himself, this is spiritual love.
For this love is reserved for us in the life after the resurrection. On consolation and joy. Bodily consolation and joy are wealth, health, strength, beauty, and the rest.
The soul's consolation is conversation about good things, reading the Scriptures, and discovering wisdom.
Spiritual consolation is expectation of the resurrection, hope in God, and knowledge of the world to come.
This joy, however, is not fully present in this life, but is reserved for us in the life after the resurrection.
On worship. Bodily worship is kneeling, bending the back, and rolling on the ground.

This act of bowing has the same outward appearance whether directed toward God or toward human beings. But because it is not fitting to worship God in the same manner in which we bow before human beings,
he requires of us, in the teaching of the Gospel, worship superior to bodily worship. He says, “Those who worship God must worship him in spirit and in truth” (John 4:24).
Worship in spirit, in our life here, is an attentive mind engaged in inward supplication, a heart crying out in longing.
Another treatment of the remaining meanings of the terms. Rather than state these three distinctions for each of these terms, those things are sufficient
that we have said explicitly about the body, the soul, and spirituality. As for the remaining things, understand them in terms of the soul's virtuous way of life.
A profitable course, my beloved, is the pursuit of wisdom. Profitable confinement is a mind that does not wander among evil things.
Debilitating bonds are senses that do not run in wisdom. A release that gives freedom is a mind not bound by desires.
Bending down from the height of knowledge is the soul's crookedness. The soul stands upright when it stands in the authority of its freedom.
The mind's wakefulness is good meditation. The soul's sleep is the cessation of good reflection.
Closeness to God is obedience to the commandments. Fellowship with God is holding fast to his love.
Patience in afflictions is relief from pains. Endurance in learning is a store of profit.
Chastity of thought is modesty of mind. True virginity is a soul that has not united itself with love of the body.
Purity of heart is not inclining toward the world. Bodily humility is an orderly appearance, together with a gentle reply.
Humility of soul is when the soul places itself in lowliness beneath everyone.
Supplication concerning things unseen is spiritual prayer. Bodily stillness is the cessation of speech.
Stillness of soul is a mind that does not struggle with its thoughts. Spiritual stillness is for the soul not to think about imagined things.
True mastery is the subjugation of evil impulses. Bodily pride is boasting about possessions. Pride of soul is boasting about knowledge.
The soul's laughter is mockery. Virtuous combat is warfare against the passions. True athletic achievement is victory over evil thoughts.
The soul's victory, however, is the true kingdom. The mind's armor is the clothing of wisdom. Profitable trade
is instruction about good things. Lasting wealth is a hidden treasury of the soul.
Courage worthy of praise is for a person to overcome his evil will. For even demons can bear the weight of things.
Their strength enables them to demolish walls and kill people. But they are unwilling to overcome the hostility of their envy.
This, my dear friends, is strength of soul: when it hears the opinions of heresies, it neither stumbles nor hates those who express them.
But if it hates them, this is weakness of soul. Just as the body suffers from a wound, so the soul is weakened by stumbling.
Dissipation and greed, when mixed with a fleshly outlook, mean that a person is never satisfied with the evils of others.
The soul's natural appetite is never to be satisfied with the study of wisdom. Thirst for spiritual mysteries is the delight of new life.
For just as bodily delight consists in a person not becoming full of the world's fine foods, so never being satisfied with the wisdom of that world
is a spiritual delight that gives rest and joy to the inner person. Bodily freedom is the absence of denial and falsehood toward the true word,
and being faithful in what has been entrusted to one. Freedom of soul is release from the body, not enslavement to a fleshly outlook.
Yet, my dear friends, this is certainly not the freedom of life after the resurrection if, in its searching, the soul is still enslaved to distracting passions.
For the soul that is not free from everything and is the likeness of God in its mind
has not yet attained the freedom of Christ, who is neither caught up in love for visible things nor distracted by the anxiety of searching.
For if the soul has been released from bodily passions, but has again been cast into the passions and anxieties of distraction in another form,
it has placed a yoke of slavery upon itself. Though released from the body's will, it is again, through its searching,
enslaved to creation. Through this searching it is also afraid that it may become entangled in error. For unless distracted searching ceases, fear does not cease.
But in spiritual freedom there is no enslavement to the memory of the world, no remembrance of creation, no distraction with the elements,
no investigation of their composition, no desire to know them, no love of worldly wisdom, and no opinions based on that wisdom.
Nor is that freedom enslaved to error. Rather, it is the true freedom of Christ, which is itself the kingdom of the ages—that very freedom which the ages are destined to receive.
Let us too, my dear friends, ask and plead that God, in his mercy and grace, may make us worthy of it in that communion of the ages of glory.
Therefore, my dear friends, let us approach the glorious order of the inner person's way of life. Let us distance ourselves from association with the hateful things that God hates.
Let us not let our mind settle in places of thought where there is no respite from the struggle of battle.
Let us settle our souls in a tranquil place where nothing opposes its peace. Let us not abandon our minds to thoughts that are conceived outside the will of God.
Let us join to our understanding meditation on the knowledge of the Lord of all. Let there be no negligence in us that holds our lives back from the labor of doing good.
Let us beware of the hidden sleep that has no vision of truth. Let us not leave the filth of sin in our souls,
so that they do not become ugly and lose their spiritual beauty. Let us cleanse the meditation of our hearts from the grime of worldly concerns.
Let us not abase the impulses of our souls by enslaving them to bodily comfort. Let us please God by fulfilling his will within us.
Let us not become estranged from the love of his laws through the love of sinful deeds. Let us gain the confidence to stand openly before him through sufferings endured for his name.
Let us not place ourselves under the accusation of his justice by contemptuously transgressing his law. Let us raise our lives above blame
by keeping the commandments of the righteous Lord. Let us not forfeit our adoption as children by becoming estranged from God.
Let us strive to become heirs of the Father's promises by despising the things that pass away.
Let the meditation of our hearts not grow weary with thoughts of visible things. Let us always love to meditate on things that are not set before the sight of our eyes.

Let us not become bound to anything we may possess from which we will be released. Instead, let us seek the bonds that hold our senses in the love of God, so that, when we are released from the body full of passions,
we may be found in the place of joys in God. To him be glory forever. Amen. Here ends the book of John the Solitary.
